# The Great Compilation
<note>original: "Brihat Samhita"</note>

## Composed by the Illustrious Varahamihira
<note>Varahamihira (c. 505–587 CE) was a polymath who wrote on astronomy, astrology, and various sciences.</note>

### Revised by the Illustrious Bhatta Utpala
<note>original: "Bhatta-Karna"; Utpala was a 10th-century commentator essential for preserving Varahamihira's work.</note>

---

->In the City of Calcutta<-

->This book was printed at the Baptist Mission Press.<-

->Saka Era 1786. Year 1865 of the Common Era.<-
<note>The Saka calendar is a historic Indian solar calendar; 1786 Saka corresponds to 1864–1865 CE.</note>

<term>Brihat Samhita: The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work covering architecture, weather, agriculture, and more.</term>
<term>Varahamihira: A celebrated Indian astronomer and mathematician.</term>
<term>Bhatta Utpala: A scholar famous for his detailed commentaries on astronomical texts.</term>
<term>Calcutta: The colonial capital of British India where this edition was published.</term>
<term>Baptist Mission Press: A prominent 19th-century printing house in Serampore and Calcutta.</term>
<term>Printed: Literally "marked with a seal" or "impressed."</term>
<term>Saka Era: A traditional Indian system of dating starting in 78 CE.</term>

# VARIOUS READINGS.

---

### CHAPTER I.

1. A <note>Manuscript A</note> **procreation etc.** <note>original: "प्रसूति वि०"</note>—A **possessing a thousand rays.** <note>original: "सहस्रगतमयू०"</note>—2. D **by the arrangements.** <note>original: "रचनौभिर्"</note>—4. **if** <note>original: "यदि"</note> omitted in A, B, C (text and commentary). A, S, B, N **these** <note>original: "एते"</note>; C gives and explains both readings <note>original: "rr." abbreviation for readings</note>.—5. A, D, B **having observed.** <note>original: "चालच्य"</note>—8. S **and the great** <note>original: "चन महान्"</note>—9. B, D, S, E **the science of horoscopy**, <note>original: "होराखो"</note> N **expert in the science of horoscopy.** <note>original: "होराशास्त्रवि०"</note>—S, **of discipline.** <note>original: "विनयस्य"</note>—10. S, E, N, and one manuscript <note>original: "Cod." for Codex</note> of C **of the extent.** <note>original: "विस्तरस्य"</note>—The title of this Chapter in A, B, D is: **Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Introduction to the Science," in the Compilation composed by the venerable teacher Varāhamihira**; in S **Thus the venerable...**, in N **The first chapter, titled "Introduction to the Science," by the teacher Varāhamihira** (as written); in C **Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Introduction to the Science," in the Compilation composed for the Great Festival**; at the end of other Chapters occurs **in the Bṛhat-saṃhitā** <note>The Great Compilation</note>, which, as being the most appropriate title, I have employed throughout.

### CHAPTER II.

Page 3, line 11 from the top: A, C, B, D, E **one who is not envious**, S, N **one who is free from malice**, which I have changed into **one who is free from malice.**—A **well-counseled.**—Line 15: D, S, E **possessing genius**, so N by a second hand <note>original: "sec. manu"</note>.—Line 16: N, and one manuscript of C **assembly.**—Line 18: S, E **skilled in rituals for prosperity and exorcism, conversant in knowledge and science**, N **knower of prosperity and others' exorcism, conversant in knowledge and science**, D **conversant in the rules of knowledge.**—Line 19: **knowledge** <note>original: "ज्ञान"</note> omitted in C, A, B, D.—S, E, **inquirer** <note>original: "प्रष्टा"</note> for **seer.** <note>original: "दृष्टा०"</note>—Page 4, line 1: S, E **Roma** without the **ka** suffix.—S, N **belonging to Vasiṣṭha.**—All but C, N **by the Scythians.** <note>original: "सैथ्यै"</note>—Line 2: **among the five** <note>original: "पंचसु"</note> omitted in S, E.—Line 3: S, E **authority** <note>original: "प्रमाण"</note> for **breath.** <note>original: "प्राण"</note>—C in his text: **of the parts such as the minute divisions of time**, like E, but from his explanation it seems to result that he meant, **the presiding deity of the parts such as the minute divisions of time**, like S.—Line 4: A **of the months.**—Line 7: C, B, N **division** for **distinction.**—A, S, N **of the months.**—Line 9: C, N **writing** for **line.**—Line 10: **was born** <note>original: "जज्ञ"</note> omitted in C, N.—Line 13: C, N **of the predictions of the years.**

## CHAPTER III.

1\. A, B, D, N, and one Codex of C, read **Aslesha** for **Ashlesha** <note>A common phonetic variation in Sanskrit manuscripts between 's' and 'sh'</note>. — All but C read **"certainly giving repeatedly."** — 2. E, and one Codex of C read **"beginning with Cancer."** — N, and perhaps C read **"absence of what was said."** — 4. S, E read **"upon reaching Cancer,"** A reads **"not having reached Cancer."** — E reads **"Lord Rama."** — 6. S reads **"nation,"** E reads **"wicked."** — N reads **"he destroys"** for **"that [he] destroys."** — S reads **"always the kings."** — 7. S reads **"story"** for **"place."** — 9. C in his text reads **"crushing the peaks,"** like A, S, B, D, but afterwards reads **"touching the peaks,"** like E. — 10. A, N read **"burnings."** — 11. E reads **"and if the sight,"** N reads **"if indeed."** — 12. All but C, N, E read **"and"** for **"around."** — 13. A, S, B, D read **"the sages say..."** — 14. All but N, E read **"breath."** — N reads **"eaten"** for **"flame."** — N reads **"fear"** for **"depressed."** — 15. S reads **"another's king."** — N, E omit **"and."** — C, S, E, N read **"done in the past"** — E reads **"they say,"** A reads **"they speak,"** S reads **"they declare."** — 16. S reads **"without..."** — 17. **"Would be"** is omitted in S, E. — S reads **"in the form of."** 18. N reads **"with smoke and flames."** — 19. A, S, E, B, D read **"the sun is the color of the sky."** — 20. All but C, N, E read **"situated in the disk."** — 22. C reads **"he does not do it for twelve years."** — 29. E reads **"in the absence of."** — E, N read **"whoever [sees] a hole in the sun."** — 31. C reads **"sound"** for **"harsh"** (explained as **"noise"**), N has **"sound,"** in the others it is not clear whether it is **"harsh"** or **"own."**

### CHAPTER V.

This Chapter is in **N** the 10th, the 5th with him being the 6th of the others, and so on. 5. **N** *yadi* for *khalu*. — 8. E, **N** Purvarddha. — 9. C Parshve cha, A, B, D Parshve. — **N** Dirgha tu. — 14. **N** *samm* for *(cha)yam*, E omitted, S Purvarddha. — 15. S, **N** *(cha)ryena* for *tena* and also one manuscript of C in the text. — 18. **N** *vijneyo* for *digjneya*. — S Valato for Valanaya. — *tani* omitted in **N**, E. — 19. After this S, **N** insert the two following stanzas:

> The solar days reached in the calculation, increased by 790 and divided by 180; the remainder divided by seven gives the period starting from Brahma. <note>original: "karanagata ravi-divasah khayamanaga (790) yutah hritah khavasuchandraih (180)..."</note> || 10 || Or || The Shaka era multiplied by the sun (12), added to the months, and divided by 44; the result is the revolutions, and the remainder divided by six is the period. <note>original: "athava ravi-gunite shakakale masasamete..."</note> || 15 ||

— **N** "Auspicious for the ruler," the others "Auspicious for the rulers," but C, although writing thus in the text, explains it as "granting fearlessness" according to our reading. — 25. S, **N** "of those skilled in mathematics." — 28. S Nairritikan, **N** Naihritikan. — 29. E Pa(shan)da. — S "in the second part." — D Khe — All but S "in the third part." — 31. A, B, D "at the approaching time." — 32. All but C "the Vaishyas and Shudras." <note>The merchant and laboring classes of the caste system.</note> — S "in the south." — 33. E Shakta. — 34. **N** *jiva* <note>life/soul</note> for *bija* <note>seed</note>. — 35. ## CHAPTER XII.

The opening stanza is wanting in **C, B, E** and originally also in **G**. It is to be found in **C** only as a quotation from the author's *Samâsa-Sanhitâ* <note>A "Brief Compilation" or summary work by the author</note>. *Variant readings are*: (**C,**) **D, G** Vatapo.—(**C**) by the bellies; **G** by his own belly.—**D** Pola, of the expanse of the ocean's water, great, and belonging to the south.—(**C**) the essence of the water's splendor; **D** the essence made of the water's splendor; **A, S, G** today the essence of good deeds has been made by me; "made" is in the Genitive case.—1. **E** by the ocean-risings.—**G** heap for nail.—**S** consisting of pearls for consisting of jewels.—3. **S** hanging for placed, **A** *by the first hand* hanging.—6. **A** her body adorned with the jewelry of her lover...—**E** long-armed...—**C** excessive for towards.—**D** beautified by the raising of banners, **S** the beauty of the raising of banners in the city, **E** the same, but *omitting* city.—**N** the temple of an elephant.—**A** mixed with the delusion of rut...—**A** *by the second hand*, and **B** with the low humming sounds sung by swarms of bees, **G** *by the first hand* with the low sounds touched by the sight of swarms of bees, *second hand* added "sung" before "touched," **N** with the low sounds touched and sung by the sight of swarms of bees, **S** the same, but "low," **E** with the sounds gone low by the rows of bees, **C** with the low sounds touched by the swarms of bees.—**A** *omits* tiger.—**A, S, D** dwelling in the heaven-like forest, **N** practicing in the heaven-like forest.—**A** near the various waters, **D** near the path of the waters, **E** endowed with the supreme joy of the end of the water's path and the fruitfulness of the Brahmins.—**S** honored for worshipped.—7. All but **C** consisting of flowers.—8. **E** speech.—**C** nourishing, *explained by* "causing to thrive"!, **A** filling.—**A** robbed of jewels.—**S** moving, the others "sexual play," which I have changed into "river."—9. All "autumn," changed by me into "river."—11. **E, G** scattered for full.—**S** of the clouds.—**A** by name.—13. All but **A, S, N** wealth for an offering of honor.—14. **A** thus for and that.—All but **E** in Ujjayini.—15. **C** divisions.—**C** once "value," once "offering."—16. **C, N, G** by foods, although **C** *explains it as* "by cakes and such."—17. **C, D** this offering.—All but **C, N** we give.—All but **G**

->CHAPTER XLVIII.<-
<note>This chapter concerns the "Pushya-Abhisheka" or the Royal Bathing Ceremony performed under the asterism Pushya.</note>

1. A, S, B, and D read *upaghātasaṃsthānāt*. — A reads *cintaṃ*. — 2. N and E read *pūṣṇa tāṃ*, B and D read *purataḥ*, which is also found in the margin of A. — 3. It is impossible to make out whether the manuscripts intend *Puṣa* or *Puṣya*; the only Bengali Codex, E, gives here *Puṣya*, and afterwards *Puṣa*. The commentator Utpala most decidedly says: "*Puṣyasnānaṃ* is the bathing performed during the Pushya lunar mansion <note>original: "nakshatra"</note>"; nevertheless, at verse 38 he explains the word as *oṣadhisnānaṃ* <note>original: "herbal bath"</note>. It remains doubtful to me what the exact form of the word was as written by Varāha Mihira, but there is no doubt about the original form, which is *Puṣyasnānaṃ*, as appears from verse 82, where its synonym is "The Propitiation of Pushya" <note>original: "Pauṣī śāntiḥ"</note>. Still more explicit is a quotation from the ancient sage Vṛddha-Garga:

> "For the sake of the inauguration of Indra <note>original: "Purandara"</note>, the preceptor Brihaspati arranged this propitiatory rite <note>original: "shanti"</note> under his own lunar mansion, of which Brihaspati is the presiding deity. (Variant in another Codex: The lunar mansion is declared to be Pushya, of which Brihaspati is the deity.) By that rite, the god Indra was inaugurated as the King of Gods. Then, having gathered strength, he destroyed the demons <note>original: "Danavas"</note>. The gods, with joyful minds, then reached the city of Amaravati. From that time forward, the strength-giving Pushya-bath was established."

— 5. C and N read *pratānānvite*. — 6. C reads *parāpata*. — 7. A reads *kokilādi°*. — E reads *cetvāgāreṣu cāpyathavā*. — 8. A and D read *vicitreṣu*, S reads *vīcitreṣu*. — All manuscripts except S read *dṛgmanasoḥ*. — A, S, and a second hand in N read *protphullahamsa* <note>original: "blooming swans"</note>, one Codex of C reads *pronnatahamsa*, another as in our text, D reads *prodbhuta*. — E reads *kuvara*. — A reads *sphulendīvara*. — 10. D reads *kaṇa* for *svana* <note>original: "sound"</note>. — B and D read *prodvignaku°*, (C notices a variant reading *proddhṛtku°*). — 11. E reads *vandita* for *valgita*, the others, barring N, read *vallita*, but C explains it as *krīḍita* <note>original: "played" or "sported"</note>. — 12. C and N read *ratnapāta*. — 13. E reads *mṛgā°*, S reads *mṛgayā°*. — C, D, and E read *yeṣu* for *yatra*. — 14. E reads *varṇa* for *valgu*. — 16. One Codex of C reads *svapna*? for *svaca*, explained as *khaḍā* <note>original: "chalk" or "grass"</note>, another Codex however reads *svaca*, explained as *garta* <note>original: "hole/ditch"</note>; B reads *svaca* or *khacakarkarā*. — D reads *svāviṭ*, A and N read *svāviṇ*, S reads *svāvidā*. — C and E read *muṣika* <note>original: "mouse"</note>. — 17. C and N read *eṣā* for *evaṃ*, D and E read *eṣāṃ*. — All but C and N read *yathāyogyaṃ* <note>original: "as is fit"</note>. — 18. C, A, and E read at the end *ca* for *vā*. — 20. D reads *dvijā nagāstraiśca*, E reads *dvijāḥ sanāgāstra*.

> He opens his eyes wide, touches his shriveled belly with his hand,
> He looks far off at what is standing right next to him again.
> He wanders outside in the sunshine, but the man remembers nothing (- -)

> "My eldest son, who is a youth, applied ghee to my head"—

> But the old man here seeks friendship with them; he tells stories of faithful wives.
> In front of his wife, he says "I am performing a vow that clears the path,
> a beautiful practice for which I am fit."
> "There is no virtuous man like me among great men,
> and no faithful woman like you in the world, O sinless one."
> Lust is unceasing and virtue is obtained—
> Thus a man prattles on excessively, usually when an old man is in front of a young woman.
> He becomes angry without cause; he desires the bow of the proud.
> When told "You will be the lover of another," he says "Yes!"
> "By turns, O broad-hipped one, today my mind is troubled, I have no sleep."
> Usually, a man brings on old age by obtaining a harsh woman.

### Verse 5
With the force of Jambula flowers, poison, honey, and the swaying dark blue water-lilies; with the beauty of Padhalaka flowers and the blossoms known as Kuvalaya; with green vitriol <term>kasisa: iron sulfate used in dyes</term> and bees; with the juice of Nirgundi seeds and flowers <insert>N reads: juice of other flowers</insert>, sesame, and honey; by the overcoming of the forest beauty, with flowers of the Madana plant and Akakina roots...

### Verse 6
With Madder <term>manjistha: a red dye root</term>, Kantakari, Kapijapa flowers, and copper-colored leaves born in the grey middle; with fruits seized by the rains; with dry boar-seeds saturated with resin; with Kimshuka and lotus petals; with black grains <insert>N reads: with mud instead of petals</insert> and Sinduvara—all these held together like glass...

### Verse 7
The oil from the cooked ingredients should be placed quickly in a pure vessel, or ideally in a vessel made of the Asana tree. After performing purification on an auspicious day, this nasal medicine <term>nasya: medicine administered through the nose, often used in Ayurveda for head-related issues</term> should be applied. After pulling out the white hairs, it should be applied to the hair follicles for many days.

### Verse 8
Then one should eat nutritious food mixed with pure black gram <note>original: "masha"</note> resembling the throat of a peacock; oily food, or black gram alone for a moment. For those whose hair has become a collection of white like the swan, the moon, the stars, or a white yak-tail fan, by the application of this method, their row of hair becomes like a young black bee.

### Verse 9
And others whose hair is seen to be sparse or grey due to the mixture of white substances—those hairs played with impetuously and mercilessly by passionate women—for them, the hair becomes wide, hanging, and abundant like a thick garland, possessing the luster of a mass of darkness, black ointment, or a swarm of young bees.

### Verse 10
Because of which a white-born horse or a royal swan or any other auspicious thing is increased in color by men; having done that quickly in this world, being free from fear, they steal away [the whiteness]. This is called "Coloring Oil" <note>original: "Varnatailam"</note> or "Gorochanakhya" in the work of Charaka <note>original: "Charakakhyam"</note> by the people here.

This Chapter precedes in manuscripts A and S our 80th Chapter. — 2. It gives a historical story. And it gives a cover for the surface of a bed. But some desire 'the spreading of the story.' 'Katha' means a woolen blanket, that is the covering. This is the Doshaka metre.</gloss> <note>Utpala is here debating the name and meaning of a specific poetic meter (Doshaka or Doshaka) and how it relates to the imagery of blankets or stories.</note> In the dictionaries the name of the metre is given as **Doshaka**, whether this be right, or Utpala's **Doshaka**, I have no means to decide; but the explanation, and especially the words **in the sense of the word 'atha'**, leave no doubt that Utpala called the metre **Doshaka**; if the variant reading I have preferred be correct, the author called the metre **Dosha**.

<meta>This page introduces the preface to the Bṛhat-Saṃhitā, establishing the historical context and lineage of the author, Varāha-mihira.</meta>

# PREFACE.

->— ❧ —<-

The name of <term>Varāha-mihira</term> <note>A celebrated 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note> must be familiar to every <term>Sanskrit</term> scholar from the writings of <term>Colebrooke</term>, <term>Davis</term>, <term>Sir William Jones</term>, <term>Weber</term>, <term>Lassen</term>, and, not least, from the writings of <term>Albírúní</term> <note>Al-Biruni, the Persian scholar who studied Indian science in the 11th century</note>, brought to public notice by <term>Reinaud</term>. But, however well known the name of the <term>Hindu</term> astronomer and astrologer may be, his works are disproportionately less generally known, because with one exception they existed only in Manuscripts and were consequently accessible to comparatively few. It is with the desire of extending that knowledge that I have undertaken the editing of the most celebrated of <term>Varāha-mihira’s</term> works, the <term>*Bṛhat-Saṃhitā*</term> <note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work covering astrology, planetary movements, and natural divination</note>.

<term>Varāha-mihira</term>, or, as the name is also written, <term>Varāha-mihara</term>, was a native of <term>Avanti</term> <note>An ancient Indian kingdom, modern-day Malwa</note> and the son and pupil of <term>Ādityadāsa</term>, likewise an astronomer.* The statement of <term>Utpala</term> <note>A 10th-century commentator on Varāha-mihira's works</note> that he was a <term>Magadha Brahman</term>† must most likely be understood in this sense, that his family derived its origin from

---

\* We have for this his own testimony in the <term>*Bṛhaj-jātaka*</term> <note>The "Great Birth Chart," a foundational text on natal astrology</note>, Ch. 26, 5:

<note>original Sanskrit: "आदित्यदासतनयस्तदवाप्तबोधः कापित्थके सवितृलब्धवरप्रसादः। आवन्तिको मुनिमताण्यवलोक्य सम्यग् होरां वराहमिहिरो रुचिरां चकार ॥"</note>

“<term>Varāha-mihira</term>, a native of <term>Avanti</term>, the son of <term>Ādityadāsa</term> and instructed by him, having obtained the gracious favour of the sun, at <term>Kāpitthaka</term>, composed this elegant work on Horoscopy, after making himself duly acquainted with the doctrines of the ancient sages.” It may be also that <term>Kāpitthaka</term> is the place where he received his education; it is the name of a village, according to <term>Bhaṭṭa Utpala</term>, the excellent commentator of <term>Varāha-mihira’s</term> works.

† Cf. <term>Colebrooke</term>, Algebra, p. XLV. foot-note.

<summary>The editor introduces the 6th-century astronomer Varāha-mihira, noting that while his name is famous among Orientalists, his primary works like the Bṛhat-Saṃhitā have remained largely inaccessible in manuscript form. The text establishes the author's lineage as the son of Ādityadāsa and his origins in the region of Avanti.</summary>

Magadha; up to the present day it is a common practice in India, for Brahmans <note>The priestly and scholarly class in the Hindu social hierarchy.</note> to be distinguished by the name of the country whence they themselves or their forefathers have come; so that, in Benares for instance, there are Kányakubja Brahmans, Mahratta Brahmans, Drávida Brahmans, &c., many of whom have never seen the country of their forefathers. As Utpala <note>A 10th-century commentator on Varāhamihira's works.</note> repeats his statement, I think it improbable that the words Magadha Brahman are an error of the manuscripts for Maga Brahman, the name given to the sun-worshippers, although this would not unnaturally suggest itself at first sight.

No information is to be found in the works of our author which have come to us, about the year of his birth, nor could we expect to find it but in his astronomical treatise *Panca-siddhántiká* <note>Literally "The Five Astronomical Canons," a vital historical text summarizing earlier Indian astronomy.</note>, which unhappily seems to be lost beyond hope of recovery. There is every reason to believe that we should find the author's date in that treatise, because it is the all but universal practice of the scientific Hindu astronomers to give their own date. In one way or another the Hindu astronomers at Ujjayaní <note>A major center of mathematical and astronomical study in ancient India.</note> must have had means to know the date of Varáha-mihira, for in a list furnished by them to Dr. Hunter <unclear>and</unclear> published by Colebrooke,* the date assigned to him is t<unclear>he</unclear> year 427 of the S'áka-era <note>An ancient Indian calendar system beginning in 78 AD.</note>, corresponding to 505 A. D.

It is not added to what period of his life this <unclear>d</unclear>ate refers. The trustworthiness of the Ujjayaní list is not only exemplified by the fact that others of its dates admit of verification, but also in a striking manner by the information we get from Albírúní <note>A famous 11th-century Persian scholar who traveled to India and wrote extensively on its science.</note>. This Arabian astronomer gives precisely the same date† as Dr. Hunter's list eight centuries afterwards, from which it is evident that the records of the Hindu astronomers have remained unchanged during the lapse of more centuries than there had elapsed from Varáha-mihira till Albírúní. The latter adds, what is not stated distinctly in the Ujjayaní list, that 505 A. D. refers to the author's *Pancasiddhántiká*. This state-

The argument would, on the grounds of analogy, seem to be corroborated by Dr. Hunter's list; for at least two other dates—those of <term>Bhaṭṭa-Utpala</term> <note>A 10th-century commentator on astronomical texts</note> and <term>Bhāskara-ācārya</term> <note>A leading 12th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>—can be verified. Since these dates refer to specific works by these authors rather than their birth years, it is natural to assume the same applies to <term>Varāha-mihira</term> <note>A 6th-century polymath and astronomer</note>. There are, however, two facts that make the date assigned to the <term>Pancasiddhāntikā</term> <note>Varāha-mihira's "Treatise on the Five Astronomical Canons"</note> not necessarily incredible, but certainly improbable. 

The first is the date of <term>Varāha-mihira</term>'s death, recently determined by Dr. Bhau Daji to be 587 A.D. The second difficulty is that <term>Varāha-mihira</term> quotes <term>Aryabhaṭa</term> <note>The famous 5th-century mathematician-astronomer</note> in a work that must have been the <term>Pancasiddhāntikā</term>.* Since <term>Aryabhaṭa</term> was born in 476 A.D., it is unlikely that by 505 A.D.—only 29 years later—his work would have achieved such fame that <term>Varāha-mihira</term> would cite it as an authority. While not impossible, it is improbable. Conversely, the error made by <term>Albīrūnī</term> <note>The 11th-century Persian scholar and traveler</note> in mistaking 505 A.D. for the date of the <term>Pancasiddhāntikā</term> when it was actually the author's birth year is easily explained. 

Inferences drawn from astronomical data prove beyond doubt that <term>Varāha-mihira</term> could not have lived long before 500 A.D., yet these data are neither numerous nor precise enough to fix a date more exactly. It is impossible to eliminate observation errors from just one or two data points, and it is often necessary to make assumptions to reach any conclusion. For a full discussion of these data, I refer the reader to Colebrooke's *Algebra*.†

Although not able, as yet, to fix the date of Varāha-mihira's birth with precision, we know with certainty that <unclear>the</unclear> <unclear>most</unclear> flourishing period of his life falls in the first <unclear>half</unclear> of the 6th century of our era. This point, important in itself, has the additional value that it serves to determine the age of other Hindu celebrities whom tradition represents as his contemporaries. The trustworthiness of the tradition will form matter for discussion afterwards; let us assume at the outset that the tradition is right, then it will follow that his contemporaries were Vikramāditya, the poets and literati at the court of this king, especially Kālidāsa and Amara-sinha, and it may be added from another source, the author of the *Pancatantra* <note>A famous ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in Sanskrit verse and prose.</note>. We shall begin with Vikramāditya, and since there are more princes than one who bore that name, or title, we shall have to enquire, which of them may have a claim to be considered the contemporary of Varāha-mihira.

It is generally assumed that the first Vikramāditya known in the history of India, was a king reigning in the century before the Christian era, and that he was the founder of the Indian era, generally denoted by <term>Samvat</term> <note>Short for Vikram Samvat, a Hindu calendar era beginning in 57 BCE.</note>. The objections that may be raised against this opinion are so many and formidable, that no critical man can adopt the fact without submitting the

> deduce some data from the time of the heliacal rising <note>The first time a star becomes visible in the dawn sky after being hidden by the sun's brightness.</note> of Canopus, as stated in Ch. 12, vs. 14, of the <term>Bṛhat-Saṃhitā</term> <note>Varāha-mihira's "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work on astrology, weather, and architecture.</note>, is literally abused by Bentley, because he, Colebrooke, holds the heliacal rising to imply the star being visible. Bentley argues that the Sanskrit word for heliacal rising always means cosmical rising and never implies the star being visible, that Colebrooke therefore had wilfully misrepresented the passage of the *Bṛhat-Saṃhitā*. Thus then Bentley heaps abuse upon a man who takes the unwarrantable liberty of taking for granted that “being visible” means “being visible.”

Let us suppose that some European considers, however erroneously, that the begi<unclear>nn</unclear>ing of the Emperor Augustus’ reign and the beginning of th<unclear>e Ch</unclear>ristian era are contemporaneous facts; would then the o<unclear>nly</unclear> possible conclusion be this, that the man thinks that he <unclear>lives</unclear> in the year of grace 1896, instead of 1865? But let it be possible, it is not the only possibility; the man may have forgotten the precise date of Augustus’ reign, a much more probable contingency. Thirdly, it is again, imaginable, that the man places the two not contemporane<unclear>ous</unclear> facts, wrongly supposed contemporaneous by him, in a time which is wrong for both, say at the time of Pericles. The first and third conclusions are, to use a mild term, so extremely improbable that only the second is left. Let us apply it to the case of Utpala; and we shall find that the only, not preposterous, conclusion is, that Utpala places Vikramáditya 78 A. D., not 57 B. C. Now the specified date falls on a Thursday and could only do so, if the S'áka era is taken as the era which *in English* <note>original: "Anglice"</note>, not in Sanskrit, is called S'áliváhana era.*

I have assumed throughout, for argument's sake, that Utpala <note>A 10th-century commentator on astronomical texts</note> was wrong in making Vikramáditya <note>A legendary emperor of ancient India often associated with the founding of eras</note> the founder of the S'áka era <note>An era beginning in 78 AD, widely used in Indian astronomy</note> because I had to show that, whether rightly or wrongly, he placed Vikramáditya 78 A. Whether he is right in doing so is a question apart which we shall discuss afterwards; first we have to revert to Lassen's <note>Christian Lassen (1800–1876), a leading German Orientalist of the time</note> remarks concerning Brahmagupta <note>A famous 7th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>. This astronomer, says Lassen, reckons from the S'áliváhana era; that is true, but apt to mislead; he reckons from the S'áka era, which Europeans persist in calling S'áliváhana era. Moreover not only does Brahmagupta reckon from the S'áka era, but all other astronomers do so. The only inference from the facts, that Brahmagupta reckons from 78 A. D. and that the same Brahmagupta places in that year the end of the S'aka kings, is that his testimony agrees with that of Utpala, barring that he does not give the name of their conqueror. The stricture upon the commentator, who erroneously brings forward Vikramáditya, is begging the question; it ought precisely to be shown that Vikramáditya did not live at that time. Arguments of a different kind are required, before the authority of the Hindu astronomers is shaken.

As harmless as this attack upon them, is the attack upon Kalhaṇa-Paṇḍita <note>The 12th-century author of the Rajatarangini, a chronicle of the kings of Kashmir</note>, the historian of Kashmere. Let us see what charges are brought against him.

The author of this production places, indeed, <term>Vikramáditya S'akári</term> at 57 B.C., but I shall show that he is an impostor, and a very clumsy one, so that his word cannot carry much weight. To those who know the work, such a task may seem not requisite, but as the spuriousness of the <term>Jyotirvidábharana</term> has been inferred from other grounds, a new discussion on its merits will not be deemed wholly superfluous.

The author professes to be no less a person than the renowned <term>Kálidása</term> <note>The most famous classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist</note>. It would be a tedious task to enumerate all the reasons, why the work must be an impudent fabrication, although every line affords examples "to the point of nausea" <note>original: "nauseam usque"</note>; moreover one passage decides all. The passage is given at length by Fitz-Edward Hall* whose remarks may be compared. There the <term>Pseudo-Kálidása</term> <note>A term used for an author falsely claiming to be Kalidasa</note> tells us, that he lived at the court of <term>Vikramáditya</term>, the king of <term>Málava</term>, who slew 555,555,555 <term>S'akas</term> <note>The Shakas or Scythians, nomadic people from Central Asia</note>;† that amongst others, at the same court, lived <term>Varáha-mihira</term> <note>A famous 6th-century astronomer; his presence here creates a chronological impossibility if the king lived in 57 BCE</note>. Further it is said that the <term>Jyotirvidábharana</term> is written in the

As the temple, according to the inscription before mentioned, was erected by Amara-Deva, one of the nine gems at the court of Vikramaditya, he concludes that Amara-Deva is the same with Amara-Sinha, the author of the *Amara-Lexicon* <note>original: "Amara-Kosha," the oldest surviving Sanskrit lexicon</note>, and that the same Amara-Sinha must have lived between 400 and 600 A.D.; taking the mean, we get 500 A.D., which again coincides with what we should expect in regard to Varaha-mihira.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the historical dating of Sanskrit literature, specifically responding to the skepticism of John Bentley regarding the antiquity of the Panchatantra.</meta>

the specious ground that the passage in the *Panchatantra* <note>A famous ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in Sanskrit verse and prose.</note>, as it stands now, might be an interpolation <note>A later insertion into a text that was not part of the original work.</note>. Bentley's objection seems to me utterly nugatory <note>Trifling or of no value.</note>, and, well analysed, amounts to this, that the interpolation of passages is a physical possibility, which is true enough, but of no use in argument. It is not enough to say that a passage may be an interpolation; any passage in any book, which is in disagreeable conflict with one's crotchets <note>A peculiar or stubborn personal belief.</note>, may then be called an interpolation. One has to give at least plausible arguments that there is something suspicious about it. Bentley has failed to do so, and wisely, for the passage in the *Panchatantra* has nothing suspicious about it. If one wishes to be sceptical, one had better doubt the whole story about the translation into *Pahlavi* <note>Middle Persian language.</note> by the command of *Shah Nushirvan* <note>Khosrow I, the Sassanid King of Persia (reigned 531–579 AD).</note>. It is many degrees less improbable that a poet, like *Ferdowsi* <note>The celebrated Persian poet and author of the Shahnameh.</note>, invents or modifies a story than that an appropriate, almost necessary, passage is to be held spurious.* In short, I think *Colebrooke* <note>Henry Thomas Colebrooke (1765–1837), a pioneering English Orientalist.</note> was perfectly right in placing the composition of the *Panchatantra* in the first half of the 6th century.

The results of the foregoing disquisitions may be summed up as follows: the first half of the 6th century, say 500—550 A.D., is in reality the most illustrious period of *Sanskrit* literature; at that time the nine gems <note>The "Navaratnas," a group of nine extraordinary scholars and poets at a royal court.</note> flourished under the patronage of an art-loving prince, and contemporaneous with them, probably in the *Deccan* <note>The southern plateau region of the Indian subcontinent.</note>, lived the author of the *Panchatantra*. The prince is either *Bhoja*, or *Vikramaditya*, or both names have to be considered as denoting the same person.—And now we have to return to our author and his works.

before him, was divided into three branches.* So we know from the *Bṛhat Saṃhitā* <note>The "Great Compilation," a foundational 6th-century Sanskrit text on astrology and divination by Varāhamihira.</note> Chapter I, verse 9:

> “The Science of the Stars <note>original: *Jyotiḥśāstra*</note>, treating of several subjects, is contained in three branches. The treatment of the whole is called by sages the Compilation <note>original: *Saṃhitā*</note>. In this science, the branch containing the movements of the heavenly bodies as determined by calculation <note>original: *gaṇita*</note> is called the System <note>original: *Tantra*</note>. The second branch is horoscopy or the casting of the horoscope.† Different from both is the third branch.”

Here then the whole of the *Jyotiḥśāstra* or astronomical and astrological science bears the name of *Saṃhitā*; the first branch is *Gaṇita* or *Tantra*, the second is *Horā* <note>The study of natal astrology or horoscopy</note>, and the third is left unnamed. Elsewhere the name for the last is the Branch <note>original: *Śākhā*</note>; so, for example, in a couplet by Garga <note>An ancient sage and legendary figure in early Indian astronomy</note>:

> “The excellent Brahman who knows the Calculation <note>original: *Gaṇita*</note>, the Nativity <note>original: *Jātaka*</note>, and the Branch <note>original: *Śākhā*</note>, is called learned in the three branches, and has completed the study of a Compilation <note>original: *Saṃhitā*</note>.”

->But one who properly understands horoscopy, mathematics, and the compendium,<-

> “But one who knows properly the **Horá**, **Ganita** and **Sanhitá**, him ought the king to honour and to secure his service, if he wishes to be victorious.”

I think we may account for the ambiguity in this way. The whole knowledge of celestial phenomena, of measuring time, of omens and portents, of augury, in short, natural astrology went under the name of <term>Compendium</term> <note>original: "Sanhitá"</note>, before each of the three branches attained its full development. When in course of time the Hindus, through the Greeks, became acquainted with two separate branches of the knowledge of the stars, (the one really scientific, the others quasi-scientific), they must have felt some difficulty in incorporating the mathematical astronomy and the so-called judicial astrology into their <term>Compendium</term>. In keeping distinct the divisions, among which the second and third are different from each other not so much in matter as in method, they continued to feel, it is not unnatural to suppose, too well the etymological meaning of <term>Compendium</term> not to apply it occasionally to the whole course of the <term>Science of the Stars</term> <note>original: "Jyotihçástra"</note> or <term>Compendium of Astrology</term>.†

<term>Varāhamihira</term> <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note> distinguished himself in all the three branches of the <term>Science of the Stars</term>. Before writing the <term>Great Compendium</term> <note>original: "Brhat-Sanhitá"</note> he had composed a work on pure astronomy, and one on horoscopy, as we learn from the <term>Great Compendium, Chapter I, verse 10</term>.‡

His first and astronomical work is always designated by himself as his *Calculation* <note>original: "Karaṇa"</note> or *Calculation of the Planets* <note>original: "Karaṇa grahánám"</note>, and we know only from Bhaṭṭa Utpala, Albírúní, and others, that its title was *The Five Treatises* <note>original: "Pancasiddhántiká"</note>, a name derived from its being founded upon the five Siddhántas <note term="Siddhánta">A comprehensive Sanskrit astronomical treatise dealing with the measurement of time and planetary motion.</note>. Albírúní, in speaking of *Calculations* <note>original: "Karaṇas"</note> as a kind of astronomical work, defines them as works forming a sequel to the Siddhántas, or as Reinaud seems to interpret the Arabic word *follower* <note>original: "tábi"</note>, being subservient to the Siddhántas. That, however, is not the common acceptation of the term; a *Calculation* <note>original: "Karaṇa"</note> differs from a *Treatise* <note>original: "Siddhánta"</note> in this respect: that in the latter the calculations refer to the beginning of the Yuga <note term="Yuga">An immense cycle of time in Indian cosmology; Siddhántas use this as a starting point for calculations.</note>, while in the former they refer to the S’áka era <note term="S’áka era">A historical calendar era beginning in 78 CE, commonly used in Indian astronomical handbooks for practical convenience.</note>. As to the word itself, it means simply "calculation," as is proved by the juxtaposition of "of the planets" <note>original: "grahánám"</note>; one might say "mathematical operation." About the contents of the *Calculation* titled *The Five Treatises*, Albírúní (Memoir on India, p. 332) expresses himself thus:

> “Varáha-mihira has composed astronomical tables, in a small volume, to which he has given the title of *The Five Treatises* <note>original: "Pancasiddhántiká"</note>. One would be led to suppose that these tables contained the substance of the five aforementioned works (*the 5 Siddhántas*), and that they are substitutes for those; but that is by no means the case.”

Besides the *Great Book of Nativities* <note>original: "Bṛhaj-Jātaka"</note>, the *Great Expedition* <note>original: "Bṛhad-Yātrā"</note> and the *Great Wedding Manual* <note>original: "Bṛhad-Vivāhapaṭala"</note>, there is, in an abridged form, a *Short* or *Small Nativity* <note>original: "Laghu" or "Svalpa-Jātaka"</note>, a *Small Expedition* and a *Small Wedding Manual*. The works written before the *Great Compilation* <note>original: "Bṛhat-Saṃhitā"; see Chapter I, verse 10</note> are the larger ones, as may be inferred from the word *copiously* <note>original: "vistaratah"</note>, and the commentator Utpala says the same, whether he inferred it, as we ourselves can do, or knew it through other means.

The *Great Book of Nativities* is among all the productions of our author the most generally known and studied in India. There exist three editions of it, I understand; I have seen two, one printed at Benares, the other at Bombay, and both accompanied with the excellent commentary of Utpala. Another commentary on the *Great Book of Nativities*, more concise than Utpala’s, is known to me only from manuscripts. It is the work of a certain Mahīdhara; the text belonging to it is very good.* The abridged book on nativity, the *Short* or *Small Nativity*, also possesses a commentary by Utpala, and is, although not so common as its larger namesake, not rarely met with. It was translated by the scholar Al-Biruni into Arabic. I am not aware that there exists a printed edition, with the exception of the two first chapters, which have been edited and accompanied with a translation by the scholar Weber.†

The *Expedition* <note>original: "Yātrā"</note> or *Manual for Journeys* <note>original: "Yātrika"</note> existed also in a double form, as we know from Utpala. I possess a manuscript of it, with Utpala’s commentary, but it seems to be incomplete, as it contains only seven chapters, out of double that number. Curiously enough all the manuscripts I have seen end after the 7th chapter, and there is no trace of a break. It is uncertain whether it be the *Small* or the *Great Expedition*, <note>The original text is obscured here by a small ink smudge</note> as no indication of it is to be found; the title of the work is *The Expedition of Planetary Yokes* <note>original: "Yoga-Yātrā"</note>. About the *Wedding Manual* <note>original: "Vivāha-paṭala"</note> I can give no information at all.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Varáha-mihira's astronomical and astrological works, specifically focusing on the Brhat-Sanhitá and its historical reception.</meta>

The last part of the <term>Science of Astronomy/Astrology<note>original: "Jyotihçástra"</note></term>, the <term>Compendium<note>original: "Sanhitá"</note></term>, is delivered by the author in the work just published by me. It is commonly called the *Varáha Compendium*, but it being desirable to distinguish it from the *Brief Compendium* or succinct *Compendium* of the author, the first title is preferable. The *Brief Compendium* has not been recovered as yet, and is known to me only from the quotations of *Bhatta Utpala* <note>A 10th-century commentator on Varáha-mihira's works</note>.

The *Great Compendium* <note>original: "Brhat-Sanhitá"</note> is now-a-days little studied, if at all, in Northern India, however popular it may have been in former times. This is but natural; it teaches so many things of exceptional use and it is so pre-eminently a manual for court astrologers, that village astrologers are wise in their generation to confine themselves to their horoscopes for marriages. Now that the palmy days of petty princes are gone, a study of such works as the *Great Compendium* would not pay. For us it is exactly the richness in details to which Hindus, as a rule, are entirely indifferent, which constitutes the chief attraction of the work; for the same reasons it was so highly valued by *Albírúní* <note>The famous Persian scholar Al-Biruni (973–1048), who studied Indian science</note>. Although an astrological book, it contains important astronomical data, and its value for geography, architecture, sculpture, etc. is unequalled by any Sanskrit work as yet published. Nor is it of slight importance as regards mere Sanskrit philology.

The merits of *Varáha-mihira* as an astronomer cannot be adequately inferred from the present publication; we ought to possess the whole of his treatise before we could do him justice. In the *Great Compendium* he is in the awkward position of a man who has to reconcile the exigencies of science and the decrees, deemed infallible, of the <term>Sages<note>original: "Rshis"</note></term>.* <unclear>The</unclear> result of such an attempt is not satisfactory. Thus much is to be gathered from his writings, especially from the fragments of the *Five Astronomical Treatises* <note>original: "Pancasiddhántiká"</note>, that he belongs to the class of *Aryabhata*, *Brahmagupta*, *Bháskara* <note>Renowned Indian mathematicians and astronomers</note>. It has been supposed that he was the first to fix the Hindu sphere at the beginning of <term>the first lunar mansion<note>original: "Açviní"</note></term>, but this does not

I refrain here from entering into a description of the contents of the *Bṛhat-Saṃhitā* <note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work on omens, architecture, and natural science by the 6th-century polymath Varāha-mihira.</note>, because it can be done much more conveniently in the translation which is in preparation. Besides, the text itself is now accessible to all; as a substitute I shall give as many particulars as I have been able to collect about the authorities whom Varāha-mihira mentions in his works. The information is chiefly taken from Utpala's commentaries which, with one exception, are not accessible to everybody.

Taking only the *Bṛhat-Saṃhitā* we find mentioned Parāśara, Garga (the Elder Garga), Kāśyapa, Nārada, the *Paitāmaha-Siddhānta*, the *Saura-Siddhānta*, the *Pauliśa-Siddhānta*, the *Vasiṣṭha-Siddhānta*, the *Romaka-Siddhānta* <note>The "Roman" or "Greek" astronomical treatise, showing early Western influence on Indian science.</note>, Viṣṇugupta, Asita-Devala or Asita and Devala, Ṛṣiputra, Śukra or Uśanas or Bhṛgu, Maya, Bṛhaspati, Śakra, Garutmat, the seven Ṛṣis (the Great Bear), Bādarāyaṇa, Nagnajit, Sārasvata, a work called *Sāvitra*, another named *Ṣaṣṭyabda*, Manu, Viśvakarman, Vajra (or Vātsa, Vātsya), Śrī-Dravyavardhana (or Śrī-Vardhamānaka), Kapiṣṭhala, Bhāradvāja, and incidentally Kapila and Kaṇabhuj. To these may be added those which are quoted in other works of our author, namely Satya or Bhadatta, Manittha, Devasvāmin, Siddhasena, the Greek authors, Jīvaśarman, Lāṭa-ācārya, Siṃha-ācārya and Āryabhaṭa.

Many of the Ṛṣis <note>Sages or seers.</note> upon whose authority the doctrines of astronomy and astrology <note>original: "a-trology"; likely a printing error.</note> are held to be founded are pure myths.*

(History of Literature, p. 227) adds *kulīra* <note>Crab/Cancer</note> and *trikoṇa* <note>Triangle/Trine</note>, but these seem to be genuine Sanskrit words. On the other hand ought to be added *harija* = horizon <note>original Greek: ὁρίζων (horizōn)</note>. In the *Sūrya-siddhānta*, Book V, verse 1, this word means "longitudinal parallax," but Varāha-mihira and Utpala never use it in that sense. That it means horizon is clear, e.g. from *Bṛhat Jātaka* 5, 17: **"in the manner in which a sign comes to the horizon,"** <note>original Sanskrit: यद्यद्राशिर्व्रजति हरिज़म् (yadyadrāśirvrajati harijam)</note> i.e. "rises," where the comment says: **"it leaves the line of rising,"** <note>original Sanskrit: उदयलेखां परित्यजति (udayalekhāṃ parityajati)</note> and further on: **"and that space which is seen all around where the sky is joined with the earth is the horizon."** <note>original Sanskrit: यच्चाकाशं भूम्या सहासक्तं समन्ताद् दृश्यते तद्धरिजं (yaccākāśaṃ bhūmyā sahāsaktaṃ samantād dṛśyate taddharijaṃ)</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the personification of celestial bodies in Hindu mythology, specifically comparing the "historical" status of sages to the personified nature of the sun and stars.</meta>

# Page 30

In the case of some, such as Surya <note>The Sun god</note>, Shakra <note>An epithet for Indra, king of the gods</note>, Garutmat <note>The celestial bird Garuda</note>, Brihaspati <note>The planet Jupiter and preceptor of the gods</note>, Vasishtha, Shakra, Pitamaha <note>The "Great Ancestor," usually referring to Brahma</note>, and the Great Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major, associated with the Seven Sages</note>, it is so evident that few would deny it. But there is no difference of character between the sun, etc., and Garga, Parashara, Kashyapa, Vajra, etc. If to the generality of Hindus Garga, Parashara, and Narada are persons, instead of personifications, it is because Surya, Indra, and Pitamaha are persons in the same manner. They have the merit of being at least consistent. That there were historical persons bearing patronymics <note>Names derived from an ancestor</note> derived from Vasishtha, Garga, Bharadvaja and *all the rest* <note>original: "tutti quanti"</note>, proves as little for the historical existence of those Rishis <note>Inspired poets or sages</note>, as the undoubtedly historical existence of the Heraclidae <note>The descendants of Hercules</note> proves Hercules to have been a person, instead of the sun in his yearly course. Parashara, Garga, and Vajra are, so far as I am able to see, nothing else but synonyms of Brihaspati. Whatever opinion one may en-

<column-break/>

history of the English East India Company, on hearing the brilliant achievements of Company Bahadur <note>A title of respect; here referring to the personification of the East India Company as a single heroic figure</note> from the time of his birth till his death, during a life of about 250 years, would smile in unbelief at the absurdity of the story. Yet there is nothing absurd, nay more, the story is strictly true, provided one substitute a personification for a person. The whole of religious and not-religious mythology (for myths are by no means exclusively religious) would be perfectly true, if we had the key to them. But this is not the case as yet. The key to mythology in general has been found long ago, but not to every myth, because they were exposed to the modifications and corruptions by more or less rationalizing influences. A curious example of a palpably corrupted myth struck me in Cardwell's excellent *Dravidian* Grammar, p. 80, where it is stated that Agastya (Canopus) <note>The star Canopus, associated with the sage Agastya</note> is believed by the majority of orthodox Hindus to be still alive, "*although invisible to ordinary eyes.*" The first part is a true myth, Canopus does exist, but the second part of the myth is adulterated; it ought to be: "although not always visible," i.e. during the time of its h<unclear>elia</unclear>cal <note>The period when a star is hidden by the sun's brightness</note> setting Agastya is invisible.

There are many who are in the habit of calling the natural explanation of myths an attempt on the part of destructive criticism. To those it seems perfectly natural that generations after generations of individuals and nations have quietly sat down to frame fables which would be most stupid, preposterous and immoral, unless their meaning is unriddled by destructive criticism. Happily criticism, whether right or wrong, has the merit of holding the more charitable view.

entertain about their mythical or historical character, it is necessary to keep in view that the books which profess to derive their authority from those <term>Rishis<note>Inspired sages or seers to whom the Vedas and other ancient sciences were revealed.</note></term> are composed several thousands of years after the supposed age of the sages. For the sake of brevity, one may say <term>Garga<note>An ancient sage and astronomer often cited in Sanskrit literature.</note></term> instead of the book bearing his name, where no ambiguity can be the result.

To begin with <term>Parashara<note>A legendary sage credited with the authorship of various astronomical and mythological texts.</note></term>, he is a prominent figure in some <term>Puranas<note>A genre of ancient Indian literature consisting of history, mythology, and philosophy.</note></term>. Some information about him is gathered in Wilson's translation of the *Vishnu Purana* (edited by F. E. Hall, page 8). In the *Mahabharata* (Book I, Chapter 176) his name is *Shaktiputra*;* Varahamihira in the *Brihat Jataka* (VII. 1) calls him *Shaktipurva*. Both names convey the same meaning, *Shaktiputra* being "the son of strength," the latter "originating in, or resulting from strength." <note>original: "S'aktiputra... S'aktipúrva"</note> Weber† remarks that Parashara is considered to be the most ancient of Hindu astronomers, and that the second in order of time is Garga. Upon what this notice is based, I do not know, but he is certainly not generally represented in that way. All those mythical astronomers derive their knowledge immediately from <term>Pitamaha<note>Literally "Grandfather," a name for the creator god Brahma, here cited as the divine source of astronomical science.</note></term> or <term>Brihaspati<note>The preceptor of the gods and the personification of the planet Jupiter.</note></term>, and it is far from the intention of the epic poems, I dare say, to distinguish the Rishis in time. Where poets ascribe to their Rishis or other personifications a life of many thousand years, they think or care little about chronology. This much is certain: if one wishes to classify Parashara, Garga, the sun, etc., according to the time at which they are imagined to have lived, one must acknowledge Pitamaha as the first astronomer, he being the fountainhead of the science. That the name of Parashara has become prominent in Sanskrit literature above other Rishi-astronomers is due to his being a proclaimer of Puranas. The frequency of his name in the writings of scholars who have occupied themselves with Hindu astronomy is due to <term>Utpala<note>A 10th-century commentator who preserved many fragments of older, lost astronomical works.</note></term>. The latter, in commenting upon the passage in the *Brihat Samhita* (III. 1), where Varaha—

To judge from very numerous quotations, the greater part, at least a large part, of it is written in prose, a striking peculiarity amongst the works of its class. A pretty large part is in the Anushṭub meter <note>A common Sanskrit poetic rhythm consisting of four quarters of eight syllables each</note>, and it contains also Áryás <note>Another specific style of Sanskrit verse</note>. Interesting for the geography of India is an entire chapter which Varáha-mihira, only changing the form, but leaving the matter almost intact, has given in the 14th Chapter of the *Great Compilation* <note>original: "Bṛh.-Saṇhitá"</note>; therefore we have to consider that chapter as really representing the geography of the Paráçara-tantra or perhaps yet more ancient works, and not as the actual map of India in Varáha-mihira’s time. This does not appear from the *Bṛhat-Saṃhitā* <note>The "Great Compilation" of Varāhamihira</note>, where Vṛddha-Garga occurs twice\* and no verses are quoted, but from quotations in Utpala’s commentary. More than once the opinion of Vṛddha-Garga is set against that of Garga; for example, when at the beginning of Chapter XXXI of the *Bṛhat-Saṃhitā* the dissentient views of the Sages about the cause of earthquakes are noticed, the commentator cites some verses of Vṛddha-Garga, who represents earthquakes as caused by the gods to show their satisfaction or dissatisfaction with the conduct of the mortals; Garga on the contrary sees the cause of earthquakes in the heaving sighs of the tired elephants of the four quarters <note>In Hindu cosmology, eight elephants (Diggajas) support the world at the cardinal and intermediate points</note>. This is not the only passage. Sometimes Garga and Vṛddha-Garga—that is, the works quoted under these names—are both cited as authorities for some opinion in which both agree. Here we have two facts: Garga and Vṛddha-Garga, considered as persons, are one and the same, but where Utpala quotes Vṛddha-Garga he has another work than the *Gārgī-Saṃhitā* in view. As the Greek historians ascribe the greatest conquests to Demetrius and Menander, Demetrius reigning according to Lassen 205—165 B.C. or thereabout, and as Śālicūka is in the middle between Ashoka's death, 226 B.C., and Brihadratha's death 178 B.C., it would not appear far from the truth to place the conquest of the Greeks about 195 B.C. The Gárgí-Sanhitá however goes farther; the Scythian king, who comes after, but not immediately after, the withdrawal of the Greeks, may be placed approximately 130 B.C., the aggregate of the reigns of the kings mentioned subsequently brings us down to the 1st century before our era. Asita-Devala (or, as Utpala <note>A 10th-century commentator on Indian astronomy</note> seems to mean, Asita and Devala) is one of the most celebrated of the Seer-astronomers <term>Rishi: a sage or inspired poet-seer</term>, celebrated even among Buddhists. The work ascribed to Asita-Devala has never come to my notice; from quotations I know that Asita-Devala, or at all events Devala, was acquainted with the signs of the Zodiac, from which it is to be inferred that he (I mean his work) was later than Garga.

Rishiputra seems to have been one of the chief authorities in astrological science. He is never called by any other name. From the manner in which the word is used in the Ramayana, I suspect that Rishyashringa is the mythical person intended.

He is listed as one of the eighteen proclaimers of the <term>Sanhitá<note>A "Sanhitá" is a comprehensive collection or compendium of knowledge, often covering astrology, divination, and natural sciences.</note></term> in many works that are otherwise of questionable value, though their lists certainly provide a faithful account of the most esteemed works existing at the time. Manu is represented as an authority in astrology even in a book as old as the *Gárgí-Sanhitá*, but that does not necessarily mean there was a formal book originating from his transcendental wisdom. Varáha-mihira, though mentioning Manu several times, refers to the <term>Mánava-Dharmaçástra<note>The Laws of Manu, a foundational legal and ethical text of ancient India.</note></term> only once—specifically in the *Bṛhat Sanhitá*, Chapter 74, verse 6 and following—and it is curious that only a portion of the lines he quotes appear in the version of Manu we possess today. Another passage in the *Bṛhat Sanhitá*, Chapter 54, verse 99, shows that there was a work derived from Manu, or perhaps a section of such a work, dealing with the <term>Dagárgalam<note>The science of "water-finding" or dowsing; the exploration of soil to determine where to dig wells.</note></term>. As the *Dagárgalam* regularly constitutes one of the chapters of a *Sanhitá*, it is reasonable to assume that Manu’s *Dagárgalam* was part of a larger *Mánava-Sanhitá*. I know of no such work existing today; it has likely shared the fate of many other texts for which there is little hope of recovery.

A new era in Hindu astronomy is marked by the composition of the <term>Siddhántas<note>Scientific treatises on astronomy that moved away from purely mythological explanations toward mathematical calculations.</note></term>. Three of the five standard works of that name existing before Varáha-mihira are attributed to mythical authors, and there is little doubt that their character would show traces of a transition period from myth to science properly so called. This assertion, however, cannot be proven with the materials currently at our disposal.

The *Paitámaha-Siddhánta* seems to have been entirely replaced by the revised edition created by the celebrated Brahmagupta. Even Utpala, who was so well-read in ancient astronomical and astrological literature, quotes only from the *Sphuṭa Brahma* or *Bráhma-Siddhánta*,* although he does not explicitly add the word *Sphuṭa* <note>original: "Sphuṭa" meaning "corrected" or "revised."</note>, as if it were a matter of course. Since Utpala <note>Bhatta Utpala, a 10th-century commentator on astronomical texts</note> noted that the *Paitámaha-Siddhánta* <note>The "System of Brahma," one of the five early astronomical treatises</note> had fallen into oblivion, it is not strange that Albírúní <note>Al-Biruni (973–1048), the Persian scholar who wrote extensively on Indian science</note> had no knowledge of it; see Reinaud’s *Memoir*, p. 332.

The *Saura*, or *Súrya-Siddhánta* <note>The "System of the Sun," perhaps the most influential Indian astronomical text</note> is mentioned by Varáhamihira <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note>, *Brh. Sanh.* p. 4, and Ch. XVII. vs. 1. As in the latter passage we are informed* that the treatise *Pancasiddhántiká* <note>Varáhamihira's "Compendium of the Five Systems"</note> followed the doctrine of the *Súrya-Siddhánta* in respect to the <term>grahayuddham</term> <note>literally "planetary war"</note>, an astrological name for conjunction, we may conclude that the *Súrya-Siddhánta* contained some matter which would find a place more appropriately in an astrological work. It was at least not wholly free of astrological influence, in so far that in some respects it did not disregard the terminology of the *Sanhitás* <note>Compendiums of omens and natural philosophy</note>. The *Súrya-Siddhánta*, current in the days of Albírúní, is ascribed by him to Láta, and as the Arab scholar expresses the received opinion of the native astronomers, unless where he intimates his dissent, there is every reason to believe that Láta was really, if not the original author, at least the author of the recast, as it was current in the first half of the eleventh century. Láta being anterior to Varáhamihira, as we shall see hereafter, it may be that Varáhamihira means by *Súrya-Siddhánta* Láta’s work, but for aught we know it may as well have been a still older edition, to <unclear>use</unclear> a not very adequate but sufficiently clear expression. Bhatta Utpala mentions the *Súrya-Siddhánta* comparatively very seldom, only six <term>çlokas</term> <note>poetic verses or stanzas</note> are quoted, which I subjoin in the foot-note,† because not one of them recurs in the *Súrya-Sid-*

The *Paulisa-siddhanta* <note>The "Treatise of Paulus"</note>, although not procurable now-a-days, is much better known than the foregoing, being largely quoted by several astronomers and their commentators. It stood manifestly in high favour as late as the days of Al-Biruni <note>A famous 11th-century Persian scholar who studied Indian science</note>, and was, barring the *Sphuta Brahma-siddhanta* <note>The "Corrected Treatise of Brahma" by Brahmagupta</note>, the only siddhanta he could procure for himself (Reinand, p. 334.) His testimony is, of course, the testimony of the Hindu astronomers at his time, and there is not the slightest reason to doubt its accuracy. Weber has made the suggestion that *Pulisa* the Greek may be identical with Paulus Alexandrinus, the author of an astrological work of the title of *Eisagoge* <note>Greek: "Introduction"</note>. Therefore they thought themselves not only allowed, but called upon, to modify what by observation or otherwise could be proved to be erroneous.

To return to the <term>Pauliça-Siddhánta</term> <note>A major astronomical treatise often linked by scholars to Greek influences, specifically the name Paulus</note>, it must have existed, like some of the other <term>Siddhántas</term> <note>Scientific treatises or established systems of astronomy</note>, in two editions. All the quotations from it are again in <term>Aryá</term> <note>A specific Sanskrit meter or verse structure</note>, which to my mind renders it probable that it was not long, say at the utmost 100 years, prior to <term>Aryabhaṭa</term> and <term>Varáha-mihira</term> <note>Two of the most influential Indian mathematicians and astronomers, active around the 5th and 6th centuries AD</note>. It is only one verse,* but quite enough to prove that even this "original" work had been adapted to the exigencies of Hindu science, for it gives the number of revolutions of the fixed stars during the <term>Four Ages</term> <note>The Yugas or vast cycles of time in Hindu cosmology</note>. Here too we must leave it undecided whether <term>Albírúní</term> <note>The 11th-century Persian scholar who wrote extensively about India</note> had the <term>Múla-Puliça-Siddhánta</term> in view, or the recast.

It would be extremely rash to deduce from these scanty details concerning the five first standard works of Hindu astronomical science any inference as to the probable period of their first composition. As an hypothesis, however, serves to direct the attention to a more definite sphere of investigation, we may roughly date the beginning of the Siddhánta period at 250 A.D., about half way between <term>Garga</term> and <term>Varáha-mihira</term>.

That Vishnugupta cannot in reality have been the author is sufficiently evident, because the method of horoscopy is thoroughly Greek, and not older than 300 B.C. At the same time, one ought not to call it a forgery without further proof; its style is not that of a bungler.

Bādarāyaṇa is likewise the professed author or teacher of a *Jātaka* <note>A term for a work on nativities or birth-horoscopes</note>, and often quoted by Utpala in his commentary on the *Bṛhaj-Jātaka* <note>The "Great Birth Story," a foundational text of Indian astrology by Varāhamihira</note>. The work is in *Áryá* <note>A specific Sanskrit poetic meter</note> and exhibits many Greek words, amongst which are *ápoklima* <note>original: "ápoklima"; from Greek apoklima, meaning a declining house in astrology</note> and *panaphara* <note>original: "panaphara"; from Greek epanaphora, meaning a succedent house</note>.

Nagnajit composed a work on architecture, sculpture, painting and kindred arts; Viçvakarman <note>The divine architect of the gods in Hindu mythology</note> inspired a book on architecture; so, it seems, also Maya <note>A legendary architect and king of the Asuras</note>.—Śrī-Dravyavardhana, <margin>A doubtful variant reading has Śrī-Vardhamānaka.</margin> a prince of Avanti, evidently an historical person, was celebrated as an author on augury or <term>çākuna</term> <note>The science of interpreting omens, particularly the cries and flights of birds</note>.—About the rest I have nothing to offer.

In the *Bṛhaj-Jātaka*, we find, besides some of those named above, Satya "the truthful," another name of whom, according to Utpala is Bhadatta "given by the stars," the latter formed after the analogy of Devadatta <note>"Given by God"</note>, Yajnadatta <note>"Given by Sacrifice"</note>, etc. Both appellations look as if they were fictitious. His work, although prior to Varāha-mihira's, seems not to have been much older; the metre is *Áryá*; it seems moreover to have been a genuine Indian production (if any book on Nativity may be called so), for his opinions now and then are contrasted with those of the Greeks. Concerning Jívaçarman, Siddhasena, Devasvámin, I have found nothing worth mentioning. The writings of the Greeks, "the ancient Greeks," as Utpala qualifies them, in contradistinction to Yavaneçvara Sphujidhvaja <note>Literally "Lord of the Greeks," a title for a ruler of the Indo-Greeks who translated Greek astrology into Sanskrit</note>, were so rare already in the days of the aforementioned commentator, that he had never seen them. It may be questioned whether books in Sanskrit are meant, and not in Greek. Utpala knew from other sources that the "ancient Greeks" did not reckon from the <term>S'áka era</term> <note>An Indian calendar system beginning in 78 AD</note>, naturally enough, and thinks that Yavaneçvara was the first to use the S'áka. The latter statement seems

very problematical, for it would follow that Yavaneçvara <note>Lord of the Greeks; likely a title for a Greek official or author in India</note> preceded Varáha-mihira <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note>, of which there is no indication whatever. Secondly, if he was prior in time, it is hardly to be explained why an author held so high amongst Hindu astrologers, is never noticed, nor alluded to by Varáha-mihira.

A curious name is Maṇittha, whom Weber <note>Albrecht Weber, a prominent 19th-century German Orientalist</note> suspects to be Manetho, the author of the *Apotelesmata* <note>A Greek astrological poem attributed to the Egyptian priest Manetho</note>. If I had been able to get the *Apotelesmata*, I should have compared the quotations from Maṇittha. It will be always worth while doing so, although it is not to be expected that the marked and special coincidences will be numerous or conclusive. In the same manner as a few traditions sufficed to enable Hindu astrologers to father the children of their own brains on their holy sages, so, I strongly suspect, they also did with the more renowned of the Greek astrologers. The notion of the productions of a man’s mind being his property, a notion carried to such a ridiculous extent in Europe, was unknown to them. Unhappily, the opposite extreme they fell into, is much more pernicious. In Maṇittha, as quoted by Utpala <note>A 10th-century commentator on astronomical works</note>, there is an extremely absurd passage, where the author ascribes antiquity to himself! “*Thus we, the ancients, speak;*” <note>original: "iti brúmas’ cirantanáh;"</note> that shows the spirit.*

The manuscripts in which the name occurs prove nothing; they will in one line write Áryabhaṭa and Áryabhaṭṭa, and would, if we had no other means of arriving at the truth, balance each other. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Sanskrit mathematical and astronomical manuscripts, specifically focusing on the numbering conventions of stanzas in the works of Aryabhata and the Sankhya philosophy.</meta>

The <term>Dashagiti</term> <note>Sanskrit: "Ten Stanzas of Giti"; a foundational astronomical text by Aryabhata</note> contains twelve stanzas, but we have to deduct the invocation and the colophon <note>The concluding statement in a manuscript providing facts about its production</note>, so that the remainder corresponds to the name “Ten stanzas.” It is a common, if not universal practice, not to take into account the invocation, nor the colophon, although in our manuscripts such verses are numbered as if they formed part of the body of the work. To give one out of many instances, the <term>Sankhya-Karika</term> <note>The earliest surviving text of the Sankhya school of Indian philosophy</note> is said in the colophon to contain seventy stanzas, but with the addition of matter unconnected with the <term>Karika</term>, as such, the number of the stanzas is seventy-two.*

The <term>Aryabhata-Siddhanta</term> or <term>Aryabhatiyam</term> <note>The magnum opus of the 5th-century Indian mathematician Aryabhata</note> is a very concise book, for the whole is complete in 111 stanzas in <term>Arya</term> metre <note>A specific Sanskrit poetic meter based on quantity of syllables</note>. If we deduct from this number the opening and closing stanzas, and also the invocation, placed at the beginning the 2nd chapter and identical with that of the <term>Dashagiti</term>, we get 108. This number coincides so exactly with one of two significations in which the numeral <term>ashtashatam</term> <note>Sanskrit: literally "eight-hundred" or "one hundred and eight"</note> may be taken, that there can be no hesitation in pronouncing <term>Aryashtashatam</term> “the hundred and eight stanzas” to be identical with the <term>Aryabhata-Siddhanta</term>. <term>Colebrooke</term> <note>Henry Thomas Colebrooke (1765–1837), a pioneering English Orientalist</note> never having seen a manuscript of it, rendered <term>Aryashtashatam</term> by “eight-hundred couplets” (Algebra, page XXXII) and certainly <term>ashtashatam</term> may mean 800, but does not necessarily do so. That in this case it has to be taken in the other sense, is now decided by the testimony of the manuscript itself.

---

* <term>Wilson</term> <note>Horace Hayman Wilson (1786–1860), an English orientalist</note> finds it difficult to explain why the <term>Sankhya-Karika</term> should be said to contain seventy, instead of sixty-nine verses. The reason is obvious enough; verses 71 and 72 have nothing whatever to do with <term>Sankhya</term> philosophy; it is wholly fortuitous and indifferent to that philosophy that a certain <term>Ishvara-Krishna</term> <note>The 4th or 5th-century author of the Sankhya-Karika</note> composed a poem in 70 verses, but the authority for the <term>Sankhya</term> doctrine is to be sure something connected with that doctrine. This explanation is properly speaking superfluous, for it matters not at all whether <term>Ishvara-Krishna</term> is right or wrong in deeming verse 70 essentially different from verses 71 and 72, he does so. I wish <unclear>only</unclear> to point out that in doing so he is logical, and that the difficulty is of <term>Wilson</term>’s own making; so it could not be expected any commentator would deem it necessary to explain what needs no explanation.

<summary>The author clarifies the numbering of stanzas in ancient Sanskrit texts, arguing that titles like "Ten Stanzas" or "One Hundred and Eight Stanzas" refer to the core content excluding invocations and colophons. # The Works of Aryabhata

The *Aryashtashata* <note>The "One Hundred and Eight Verses," a major astronomical treatise</note> contains all the leading features of a system the difference of which from the commonly received opinions was known to us from the accounts given of it by many of the Hindu astronomers. Aryabhata’s curious system of arithmetical notation is taught in the *Dashagiti* <note>The "Ten Giti Stanzas," which outline his numerical system and basic astronomical parameters</note>, his theory of the earth revolving on its axis in the *Siddhanta* <note>A general term for a comprehensive astronomical treatise</note>, and now that we know his date, we know at the same time that a Hindu astronomer had the boldness, as Whitney <note>William Dwight Whitney (1827–1894), a prominent American linguist and Sanskrit scholar</note> puts it, to withhold his assent from the commonly received theory. Another remarkable feature of the book is that the lunar mansions or *nakshatras* <term>nakshatras: the 27 or 28 sectors along the ecliptic used in Indian astronomy to track the moon's path</term> are not taken notice of. The only word which reminds us of their existence is *Ashvayuja*, not referring to the *nakshatra*, but taken as the name of the first year in the revolution of Jupiter, whence further it may be deduced that *Ashvini* <note>The first nakshatra in the classical list</note> was the first in the order of the lunar mansions at the time the work was composed.

As yet only the two forenamed works of Aryabhata have been recovered, but we may reasonably hope that others will turn up in time. Al-Biruni <note>A 10th-century Persian scholar who wrote extensively about India; original: "Albírúní"</note> (Memoir on India, p. 371 <note>original: "Mém. sur l’ Inde"</note>) quotes a whole passage from Aryabhata “the Kusumapurian” <note>Referring to Pataliputra, modern-day Patna</note>, which must have made part of a book different from the *Dashagiti* and the *Aryashtashata*, it not being found in those two. It has been surmised by Fitz Edward Hall <note>An American Orientalist (1825–1901)</note> that there must have been two astronomers of the name of Aryabhata, a surmise which want of materials only prevented him from raising to a certainty. By my possessing a copy of an *Aryabhatakrita-Mahasiddhanta* or *Aryabhatakhyo Mahasiddhanta* <note>The "Great Treatise composed by Aryabhata"</note>, I am in a position positively to prove the correctness of Hall’s shrewd guess. The *Mahasiddhanta* is an astronomical work in 18 Chapters, and more than 600 verses in *Arya* and *Upagiti* <note>Specific meters or rhythmic structures used in Sanskrit poetry</note> in irregular succession. The verses are altogether lame and pithless. The author distinctly states that he has written his work mainly on the principles of the “old” Aryabhata, and the truth of his assertion is born out, partly at least, by his employing the great Aryabhata’s peculiar system of arithmetical notation. He informs us further that he had introduced corrections of his

->fallen into decay through various readings; they have been distinguished <insert>or improved</insert> by me in my own words.<-

> “The *Siddhánta* and other works of the old *Áryabhaṭa* are in the long course of time worn out by the study of them; they (*i. e. Siddhántádyam*) have been modified by me on my own authority.”

The author certainly calls himself *Áryabhaṭa*, but it is so extremely unlikely that two astronomers, one being the professed imitator of the other, should bear the same name, that it is far more natural to think *Áryabhaṭa* to be only the younger astronomer’s *nom de plume* <note>French: pen name</note>. It is by no means to be inferred that by assuming the name of the celebrated astronomer he intended any fraud; since the adoption of a pseudonym in writing is in India a mark of respect and an intimation that the former bearer of the adopted name is set up as a model. That *Áryabhaṭa* the younger did not attempt to impose upon others is perfectly clear from the account given about himself. I fear that it would be very difficult to show that he was as clever as he was candid. The whole book is a poor performance. The contents have been known long ago, for it is the work that *Bentley* <note>John Bentley (1754–1824), a British scholar who wrote on Hindu astronomy and was known for his skeptical views on the antiquity of Indian texts</note> pronounced to be the real *Áryabhaṭa-Siddhánta*, the other works being only fabrications.
