Davis also knew the book, but he must have had a corrupt manuscript, for he calls it *Arsha-Siddhanta* <note>The "Treatise of the Sages."</note>. So much about the *Maha-Aryabhata-Siddhanta* <note>The "Great Treatise of Aryabhata."</note>, containing the meditations of some astronomer, who wished to imitate *Aryabhata* of *Kusumapura* <note>Modern-day Patna; the original 5th-century astronomer.</note>, and followed him at a great distance, both of time and merit.

We owe the knowledge of nearly all the particulars about the predecessors of *Varaha-mihira* <note>A famous 6th-century astronomer and astrologer.</note> to *Bhatta Utpala*. This astronomer who, as we have had occasion to notice, flourished in the middle of the 10th century of our era, seems to have earned his great reputation* less by his original compositions than by his commentaries on *Varaha-mihira*. An original work of his is the *Bhattotpala-Horashastra* <note>Utpala's Treatise on Horoscopy.</note>, a very short treatise in 75 stanzas; a manuscript of which is in possession of the Berlin Library, (see *Weber’s Catalogue* 863). Not having this *Horashastra* at hand, I cannot affirm whether it be identical with a work sometimes quoted by Utpala as his own, and called *Khanda-khadaka* <note>Literally "A Piece of Food" or "Edible Morsel," a common metaphorical title for astronomical handbooks.</note>; very likely it is the same book under another title. A greater reputation has been earned by him in his capacity of commentator. It is not known if he has written a commentary on all the works of *Varaha-mihira*, but as many of these as have been brought to light are provided with one. Those I have seen myself are the *Sanhitavivriti* or *Sanhitavritti* <note>Commentary on the Compendium.</note>, the *Brihaj-Jataka-vivriti* <note>Commentary on the Great Nativity.</note>, that on the *Laghu-Jataka* <note>The Short Nativity.</note>, and that on the *Yogayatra* <note>The Expedition of the Conjunctions.</note>. Besides these, there is extant and frequently met with, a commentary on the *Shatpanchashika* <note>The Fifty-Six Verses.</note>, a work by *Prithuyashas*, the son of *Varaha-mihira*.

The merits of *Bhatta Utpala* as a commentator are held

<meta>This page continues the scholarly introduction regarding the commentary on the Bṛhat-Saṃhitá, focusing on the merits of the commentator Utpala and the manuscripts used for this edition.</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>

high, and, methinks, deservedly so. To an unusual knowledge of the astronomical and astrological writings before his time, he adds the acquaintance with some authors in other branches of learning, like <term>Caraka</term> <note>An ancient Indian physician and author of a foundational medical treatise</note>; with a stupendous memory, he combines judgment. Where he knows his deficiency, he tells us so with a candour rarely met with amongst persons of his class. So he admits, for instance, that he is only superficially acquainted with the technicalities of perfumery (<term>gandhayukti</term> <note>The traditional Indian art of blending scents and cosmetics</note>). With a profound reverence for his author, whom he considers to be an incarnation of the sun, he earnestly endeavours to explain and to elucidate the text, without taking it as a mere pretext for pouring forth his own wisdom. When a passage is ambiguous, he has recourse to the sound method of comparing the words of <term>Varáha-mihira</term> <note>The 6th-century polymath who wrote the Bṛhat-Saṃhitá</note> with those passages of more ancient authors whom he thinks him to have immediately imitated. This method has the additional value that thereby precious fragments of authors now utterly forgotten, and perhaps never to be recovered, have been preserved. The commentary on the <term>Bṛhat-Saṃhitá</term> <note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work on omens, architecture, and natural science</note> would be well worthy of being separately edited; unhappily, it is rather bulky, containing the substance of somewhat more than twenty-thousand <term>çlokas</term> <note>A specific meter of Sanskrit verse, often used as a unit of measurement for the length of a text</note>; and a still greater barrier to such an undertaking is offered by the horrible state of all the <term>Codices</term> <note>Handwritten manuscript books</note>. In a certain sense, the merely explanatory part will find a substitute in the translation of the text, which is in preparation, and the more valuable portion of the additional matter may be inserted.

<meta>This page concludes the editor's preface, detailing the relationships between the various manuscripts used and offering acknowledgments to colleagues before the final dateline in Benares.</meta>

although it shows many striking coincidences with S in that part of S where S does not coincide with A. B and D, and partly N, show manifest traces of being influenced by the commentary; A and S show, it would seem, a total independence of C, and may be considered as constituting a class apart, which can scarcely be said of B, D, N, E. The differences of C and A, S are here and there so remarkable that one might think them to exhibit different <term>redactions</term> <note>Redactions refer to different versions of a text that have been edited or revised over time.</note>, perhaps different editions issued by the author. As a general remark, applying to all the <term>MSS.</term> <note>Abbreviation for manuscripts.</note> it may be said that all of them are worse than indifferent.

It is no mock modesty that prompts me to say that, having such materials at my disposal, I look upon this first edition of the *Bṛhat-Sanhitá* <note>The "Great Compilation," a 6th-century Sanskrit encyclopedic work on astrology, planetary movements, and various sciences by Varāhamihira.</note> as an essay of an edition, rather than an edition which would require but few occasional corrections from future editors. The bad condition of the manuscripts is so bewildering, the great number of the subjects treated of is so distracting, the class of works to which the Sanhitá belongs, is so little explored, that, it is hoped, a large allowance will be made for the difficulties I had to cope with. After all, *Varáha-mihira*’s work is so interesting that the shortcomings of the editor cannot rob it of its value.

I cannot conclude without offering my sincere thanks to Prof. E. B. Cowell who was not only instrumental in furthering the publishing of the work, but, with his well-known kindness, furnished me with manuscripts from Calcutta.

Nor must I omit to say that I owe the first hint of editing *Varáha-mihira* to my honoured friend Prof. A. Weber. If the *Bṛhat-Sanhitá* proves a useful addition to the store of Sanskrit literature, Sanskrit scholars will, therefore, have to thank him in the first place. Had it not been for his suggestion, it would, perhaps, never have been undertaken, and but for his steadfast <unclear>encouragement</unclear>, it would certainly never have been brought to a close.

->Benares, 23rd March, 1865.<-

# Salutations to the Great Lord Ganesha.

---

Victorious is the Sun, the progenitor of the world, the soul of the universe, and the natural ornament of the sky. He is honored by a garland of a thousand rays that resemble molten gold. (1)
<note>original: "Savita" (Sun). The opening verse follows the tradition of Mangalacarana, an auspicious invocation to ensure the successful completion of the work.</note>

Having observed the unerring meaning of the extensive works composed by the ancient seers, I am now prepared to explain the same clearly through a composition that is neither too brief nor too voluminous. (2)
<note>original: "Prathama-muni" (the first sages/seers). The author acknowledges that while the knowledge is ancient, the existing texts are either too long or too dense for easy study.</note>

If a work is considered "good" simply because it was composed by an ancient seer, and not because it was written by a mere mortal, then what is the difference in the specific statement when the meaning is identical and only the syllables differ—provided it is not a sacred Vedic hymn? (3)
<note>The author argues for a rational approach to literature: if the information is accurate, the human authorship of a new book is just as valuable as an ancient one, as long as it isn't a divinely revealed Mantra.</note>

If the Creator himself said that the day of the Son of the Earth is inauspicious, or if a human says "Tuesday is unfavorable," what is the difference between the divine word and the human word when the meaning is the same? (4)
<note>original: "Kujadina" (Tuesday/Day of Mars). "Son of the Earth" is a common epithet for the planet Mars.</note>

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 1

->Having observed the vast expansion of the texts<-
->descended in succession from Brahma and the other creators,<-
->my endeavor is to produce this work<-
->as a concise summary of them all. (5)<-

->Indeed, this universe was once shrouded in darkness;<-
->within the waters, it took form as a golden, radiant egg.<-
->Therein, Brahma, the creator of the universe, with the Sun and Moon as his eyes,<-
->formed the two halves of the shell: Heaven and Earth. (6)<-
<note>This refers to the Hiranyagarbha or 'Golden Embryo' myth of creation found in the Vedas and Puranas.</note>

->Kapila declared "Primordial Matter" to be the cause;<-
->Kanabhuk <note>Also known as Kanada, founder of the Vaisheshika school</note> spoke of "Atoms" and other substances as the source of this world.<-
->Some claim "Time" is the cause,<-
->while others proclaim "Inherent Nature" or "Action" <note>Karma</note> to be the origin. (7)<-

->But enough, enough with these lengthy explanations!<-
->The determination of such philosophical debates is an immense task.<-
->My purpose here is to provide a definitive explanation<-
->of the various branches of the Astral Sciences. (8)<-

The Astral Science <term>Jyotisha: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term> deals with many different subjects and is established upon three pillars <term>Skandha-traya: the 'three branches' of the science</term>. The sages declare that the name for the entire body of this knowledge is the "Compilation" <term>Samhita</term>. Within these branches, that which deals with the motion of the planets through mathematical calculation is called "Systematic Astronomy" <term>Tantra</term>. Another branch is "Horoscopy" <term>Hora</term>, which deals with the determination of the effects of the stars on lives. The third branch is known as the "Natural Astrology" <term>the Samhita branch itself</term>. (9)

->The retrograde and re-retrograde motions, the settings and risings,<-
->and other states of the planets and stars have been described by me in the "Calculative Manual."<-
<note>original: "Karana" — referring to his earlier work, the Pancha-siddhantika.</note>

<summary>Varahamihira justifies his concise summary of ancient astronomical texts and defines the three-fold division of Jyotisha into mathematical astronomy, horoscopy, and natural astrology.</summary>

### Now, we shall explain the requirements for the Astrologer.

In this regard, the <term>Sāṃvatsara</term><note>A master astrologer or "one who knows the year"</note> must be of noble birth, pleasant to look upon, modest in dress, a speaker of truth, free from envy, and impartial. He should have well-knit and well-proportioned limbs and joints. His hands, feet, nails, eyes, chin, teeth, ears, forehead, eyebrows, and head should be flawless and beautiful. He should be well-built and possess a deep, noble voice. For, generally, virtues and flaws follow the physical form of the body.

Regarding his inner qualities: he must be pure, capable, bold, eloquent, and possessed of ready wit. He must know the proper place and time, be of a virtuous nature, and not be intimidated by assemblies. He should not be surpassed by his fellow students. He must be skilled and free from addictions. He should be well-versed in the knowledge of rituals for peace, prosperity, and <term>magic</term><note>original: "abhicāra"; refers to rituals intended to influence or counteract malevolent forces</note>. He must be devoted to the worship of the gods and the observance of fasts and vows. His influence should stem from the power of his knowledge, which produces wonders independently. He must be able to answer what is asked and, by divine grace, be a master of the meaning of the texts on <term>Astronomy</term><note>original: "gaṇita"</note>, <term>Omens</term><note>original: "saṃhitā"</note>, and <term>Horoscopy</term><note>original: "horā"</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the introduction to the Bṛhatsaṃhitā and begins the second chapter, outlining the ideal physical and moral characteristics required of a professional astrologer.</summary>

# The Great Compilation <note>original: "Brihat Samhita"</note> | [Chapter 2]

In the matter of planetary mathematics <note>original: "Graha-ganita"</note>, there are five systems of astronomical principles <note>original: "Siddhantas"</note>: the **Paulisha**, **Romaka**, **Vasishtha**, **Saura**, and **Paitamaha**. The astronomer must be a knower of time and space, beginning with the smallest units—the breath <note>original: "Prana"</note> and the atom of time <note>original: "Truti"</note>—up to the divisions of the day, the hour, the fortnight, the month, the season, the half-year, the year, and the Great Age <note>original: "Yuga"</note>.

He must understand the causes of the four types of months: the solar, the terrestrial <note>original: "Savana"</note>, the sidereal <note>original: "Nakshatra"</note>, and the lunar. He must be an expert in explaining the occurrence of intercalary months <note>original: "Adhimasa"</note> and omitted days <note>original: "Avama"</note>.

He must know the beginning and end of the lords of the sixty-year cycle, the Great Age, the year, the month, the day, and the hour. He must be skillful in demonstrating the similarities and differences, as well as the appropriateness or inappropriateness, of the various measurements of time such as the solar system.

Even when the astronomical systems differ, he must be capable of demonstrating the solstice's return through direct observation, using the intersection of the sun with the prime vertical <note>original: "Samamandala"</note>, and by matching the calculated degrees with the evidence of the shadow, the water-clock <note>original: "Jala-yantra"</note>, and planetary mathematics.

He must understand the causes of the fast, slow, southern, northern, low, and high motions of the planets, beginning with the Sun. Regarding the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, he must be a forecaster of the beginning, the middle, the end, the direction, the magnitude, the duration, the intensity, the color, and the region of visibility. He must also predict the future conjunctions and "wars" <note>original: "Yuddha"; a term for close planetary alignments</note> of the planets.

He must be skilled in determining the distance of each planet's orbit in leagues <note>original: "Yojana"</note> and the specific measurements for each region. He must be an expert in the geometry of time and space, including the rotation of the Earth and the circle of the stars, the latitude, the equinoctial shadow, the diameter of the day-circle, the variation of daylight <note>original: "Chardala"</note>, the rising of the zodiac signs, and the calculations of the shadow and the water-clock.

Through his ability to resolve various challenging questions and objections, his speech gains essential strength. Such a man, who speaks of a science that has been purified like gold—refined by the touchstone and the heat of the fire—is a true **Master of the Treatises** <note>original: "Tantrajna"</note>.

And it has been said:

<summary>This passage outlines the rigorous mathematical and observational requirements for an astronomer, emphasizing mastery over the five ancient astronomical systems and the ability to reconcile theory with physical observation using tools like water-clocks and shadows.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, planetary mathematics, Siddhantas, eclipses, time measurement, water-clock, Brihat Samhita, Varahamihira</keywords>

# The Great Compilation

> If he cannot explain what is connected,
> and cannot answer even a single question when asked;
> if he cannot teach his disciples,
> how can he be considered a knower of the scriptures? || 1 ||

> When the text says one thing, but the ignorant man interprets it as another,
> or performs calculations incorrectly;
> he is like a man who, intending to approach the Creator <note>original: "Pitamaha," a name for Brahma</note>,
> instead praises a common woman with the songs of a lover. || 2 ||

> When the mathematical systems <term>Tantra: the branch of astronomy dealing with mathematical calculations of planetary motions</term> are well understood,
> and the ascendant is determined by the shadow and water-clock,
> and when the science of Horoscopy <term>Hora: predictive astrology based on the hour of birth</term> is firmly mastered,
> the speech of the astrologer shall never be in vain. || 3 ||

And it was said by the noble Vishnugupta <note>An ancient authority often identified with Chanakya or Kautilya</note>:

> A man crossing the great ocean might perhaps,
> by the force of the wind, reach the further shore;
> but even a Sage cannot, even in his mind,
> reach the end of this vast ocean known as Time. || 4 ||

In the Science of Horoscopy <note>original: "Horashastra"</note> as well, one must master the strength and weakness of the signs, the half-signs, the third-parts <term>Drekkana: a decan or 10-degree division</term>, the ninth-parts, the twelfth-parts, and the thirty-degree divisions. One must determine the various types of planetary strengths derived from their direction, position, time, and movement. This includes understanding their temperaments, bodily humors, substances, castes, and behaviors. It further encompasses the moment of conception, the wonders of the time of birth, the length of life, the planetary periods and sub-periods, the eight-fold division of strength <term>Ashtakavarga: a system of calculating planetary influences</term>, and the combinations for royal power...

<summary>Varahamihira emphasizes the necessity of deep technical mastery in astrology, warning against ignorant practitioners and quoting Vishnugupta on the infinite nature of the science of Time.</summary>

# The Great Compilation
## [ Chapter 2 ]

The effects of the lunar combinations <note>original: "Chandra-yoga"</note>, the combinations of two or more planets, and the celestial configurations known as the "Heavenly" <note>original: "Nabhasa"</note> yogas; the results of planetary aspects, their strengths, and their departures; the favorable and unfavorable omens occurring at the moment of a query; and the performance of rituals such as marriages. In the context of military expeditions <note>original: "Yatra"</note>, the astrologer must understand the lunar days, the solar days, the half-days <note>original: "Karana"</note>, the lunar mansions <note>original: "Nakshatra"</note>, the auspicious hours, the rising signs, and the planetary combinations. Furthermore, he must interpret bodily tremors, dreams, the "Victory Bath" ritual, sacrifices to the planets, communal offerings, the characteristics of the sacrificial fire, and the movements of elephants and horses. He must understand the rumors within the army, the gestures of the soldiers, the strategic use of planetary positions, the various tactical means, and the auspicious or inauspicious omens regarding the encampment grounds. 

The great teachers have also declared that the astrologer must advise on the timely employment of ministers, spies, messengers, and forest-dwelling tribes, as well as the methods for capturing enemy fortresses.

> ->As if spread out before the world,<-
> ->As if painted upon the mind,<-
> ->As if poured into the heart;<-
> ->He who possesses the science of the stars in this way,<-
> ->His predictions shall never be in vain. || 5 ||<-

One who has mastered the entirety of this Compilation <note>original: "Samhita"</note> is truly a "Thinker of the Divine" <term>Daivachintaka: a high-ranking astrologer-priest</term>. These are the subjects contained within the Compilation: the movements of the Sun and other planets; their natural states and their transformations; their size, color, rays, brilliance, and shapes; their settings and risings; their paths and alternate paths; their retrograde and sub-retrograde motions; and their conjunctions with other stars and planets. 

The astrologer must also predict the effects on various countries using the "Star-Tortoise" division <note>original: "Nakshatra-Kurma-Vibhaga," a method of mapping the geography of India onto the body of a cosmic tortoise</note>. He must understand the movement of the star Canopus <note>original: "Agasti"</note> and the movement of the Seven Sages <note>original: "Saptarishi," the Great Bear constellation</note>. Other topics include the planetary domains, the arrangement of the lunar mansions, the "triangular" planetary configurations, planetary wars, and the conjunctions of planets. He must interpret the yearly rainfall, the signs of "pregnancy" in the clouds <note>an ancient meteorological theory of rain formation</note>, and the specific lunar conjunctions in the months of Rohini, Swati, and Ashadha. Finally, he must understand immediate rainfall, the blooming of flowers and creepers, halos, mock suns, atmospheric lines, winds, meteors, the "burning" of the horizons, earthquakes, the glow of twilight, and the "City of the Gandharvas" <note>a term for complex mirages or cloud formations</note>.

<summary>This page outlines the vast curriculum required of a royal astrologer, ranging from military omens and political strategy to complex meteorological and astronomical phenomena. It emphasizes that a true master must internalize the science of the stars so deeply that it becomes part of his very being.</summary>

# The Great Compilation
## [ Chapter 2 ]

The astrologer must be constantly vigilant, setting aside all other tasks to contemplate the signs affecting the world in general, every individual person, and the King in particular. These signs include: lightning strikes; fluctuations in prices <note>original: "arghakāṇḍa"</note>; the growth of crops; the festival of Indra's Banner; rainbows; <term>Vastu Vidya</term> <note>the traditional science of architecture and placement</note>; <term>Anga Vidya</term> <note>the study of physical features and bodily movements to predict the future</note>; the behavior of crows; the circles of the winds, deer, horses, and the inner regions; the characteristics of palaces and temples; the features of idols and their formal consecration; <term>Vrikshayurveda</term> <note>the ancient science of plant health and gardening</note>; the finding of underground water; the lustration of arms <note>a purification ritual for the military</note>; the appearance of wagtails; the pacification of portents; the "variegated peacock" circle; the "ghee-blanket" ceremony; and the characteristics of swords, crowns, peacocks, turtles, cows, goats, horses, elephants, men, and women. He must also consider matters of the inner apartments <note>the royal harem</note>, the marks on caskets, the wear on shoes and clothes, and the qualities of fly-whisks, staffs, beds, and seats. Furthermore, he must examine gemstones, the behavior of lamps, and the auspicious or inauspicious signs found in tooth-sticks and other everyday objects.

Because it is impossible for a single person to observe all these signs day and night, a well-compensated astrologer should employ four other experts in the field. One assistant should watch the East and South-East; another the South and South-West; another the West and North-West; and the last the North and North-East. This is necessary because portents like falling meteors appear and vanish quickly. Their effects are determined by their shape, color, glossiness, size, and their impact on planets and constellations. As the Great Sage Garga has said:

> The King who does not honor a scholar proficient in all branches and sub-branches of the science, and who is firmly grounded in both judicial astrology and mathematical calculation, meets his destruction. **(7)**

> Even those who have retired to the forest, free from possessiveness and worldly ties, still seek guidance from the astrologer who is an expert in the movements of the heavenly bodies. **(8)**

Just as the night is without a lamp, or the sky without the sun...

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 2

->...so too does a King wander like a blind man on a path without a <term>Samvatsara</term><note>A court astrologer or astronomer who "knows the year."</note>. [9]<-

The <term>Muhurta</term><note>A precise auspicious moment lasting about 48 minutes.</note>, the lunar day, the lunar mansion, and even the nectar-like solstices—all of these would fall into total confusion if the Astrologer did not exist. [10]

Therefore, a King who desires victory, fame, wealth, enjoyment, and ultimate spiritual merit must approach a learned and leading Astrologer. [11]

One who desires prosperity should not reside in a land lacking a practitioner of this science; for where this "eye" <note>The text refers to astrology as the "eye" of the Vedas.</note> exists, sin and misfortune do not remain. [12]

One who studies the science of the stars does not fall into the hells; rather, the seeker of the divine <note>original: "daivachintakah" - one who contemplates the divine through the stars.</note> attains a permanent place in the world of the Creator. [13]

The twice-born <note>A member of the learned classes (Brahmin) who has undergone initiation.</note> who knows this system both by the letter of the text and by its deeper meaning deserves to be the first to be fed at a funeral feast; he is honored as one who purifies the entire assembly. [14]

<margin>Even foreigners are honored if they possess this knowledge.</margin>
The Greeks <note>original: "Yavanas" - specifically referring to the Indo-Greeks or Westerners who influenced Indian astronomy.</note> are indeed foreigners <note>original: "Mlechha" - those outside the traditional Vedic social structure.</note>, yet this science is well-established among them. Even they are honored like ancient seers; how much more so then a learned man of the priestly class who knows the divine science? [15]

One who makes predictions based on trickery, spirit possession, or by secretly overhearing others' whispers should not be consulted; such a person is no true knower of the divine. [16]

He who claims the status of an astrologer without actually knowing the <term>Shastra</term><note>The authoritative scientific and religious treatises.</note> is a sinner who defiles any gathering; he is to be known as a mere "star-pointer" <note>original: "Nakshatra-suchaka" - a derogatory term for a pretender who can only point at stars but not calculate their meanings.</note>. [17]

He who follows the advice of such a "star-pointer" falls into the darkest hell along with that pretender who mocks the true science of the constellations. [18]

The predictions of the ignorant are like the "vows" made to a lump of clay at the city gate <note>A metaphor for superstitious or accidental success.</note>; if they happen to come true, it is purely by chance. [19]

One who gains success only by coincidence, and who delights in fragmented and disconnected talk...

# The Great Compilation

### [Chapter 2]

A king who wishes for victory should reject a man who knows only a small portion of the science; such a person is as useless as a great bull <note>original: "mahokshita" - literally a large bull, implying someone who is physically imposing but intellectually or spiritually burdensome</note>. // 20 //

However, he who thoroughly understands the three branches of astrology—**Horoscopy** <term>Hora: judicial astrology and birth charts</term>, **Mathematics** <term>Ganita: astronomical calculations</term>, and the **Compilation** <term>Samhita: natural astrology and omens</term>—should be honored by the King and welcomed into his service if he desires success. // 21 //

A single astrologer who knows the proper time and place can achieve more than a thousand elephants or four thousand horses could ever accomplish. // 22 //

# The Great Compilation (Brihat Samhita) | [Chapter 3]

->The Course of the Sun<-

At present, the Sun's solstice <note>ayana: the solar journey</note> begins with the sign of Cancer <note>Karkataka</note>, and the other begins with Capricorn <note>Mriga/Makara</note>. Any deviation from this stated rule is a perversion of the natural order; the truth of this is made manifest through direct observation. || 2 ||

The Sun's position should be tested by observing the points of its rising and setting against distant landmarks, or by marking the entry and exit of the shadow on a large graduated circle <note>a sundial or large astronomical ring</note>. || 3 ||

If the Sun turns back without having reached Capricorn, it destroys the South and the West. If it turns back without having reached Cancer, it destroys the North and the East. || 4 ||

When the Sun has passed the northern solstice and then turns back, it brings about well-being and an increase in crops. Even when following its natural course, it acts thus; however, if the Sun’s motion is unnatural <note>deviating from the calculated path</note>, it creates fear. || 5 ||

When a dark spot appears on the solar disc without an eclipse, it is a phenomenon named Tvashtha. This portends the death of seven kings and brings suffering to the people through weapons, fire, and famine. || 6 ||

There are thirty-three "Comets" <note>Ketus</note> known as the "Dark Shafts" <note>Tamasa Kilakas</note>, which are said to be the sons of Rahu <note>the shadow planet responsible for eclipses</note>.

<summary>Varahamihira describes the observation of the solstices and warns that deviations in the Sun's expected path or the appearance of sunspots (Tvashtha) serve as omens of political and natural disaster.</summary>

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 3

->The Sun<-

If the Sun appears like a glowing coal, it brings a change in the ruling dynasty; if it is accompanied by sparks or smoke, it destroys the people. <note>Verse 18</note>

A single such omen causes famine; two occurring together lead to the destruction of the king. If the Sun is pierced by these phenomena—whether they be white, red, yellow, or black—it destroys the corresponding social classes. <note>Verse 19; the colors traditionally correspond to the four social orders: priests, warriors, merchants, and laborers.</note>

From whichever direction these great portents <term>Mahotpata: extraordinary natural phenomena seen as divine warnings</term> are seen rising from the Sun's disc <note>original: "Ravibimba"</note>, danger will come to the people from that very direction. <note>Verse 20</note>

When the Sun’s rays point upward and it appears copper-colored, it destroys the commander-in-chief of the army. If it appears yellow, it kills the king's son; if white, it destroys the royal priest. <note>Verse 21</note>

If the Sun appears variegated or smoky in color, it throws the earth into turmoil through the attacks of thieves and weapons—unless it quickly brings down rain to soothe the land. <note>Verse 22</note>

The Sun is naturally copper-colored or reddish-brown in the winter; it has the hue of a lion's mane or saffron in the spring. It appears like pale gold in the summer, and white during the rainy season. <note>Verse 23; these are considered the healthy, standard colors for the seasons as opposed to the ominous colors mentioned previously.</note>

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 4: The Movement of the Moon

->**The Cause of Lunar Reflection**<-

The Moon always stays below the Sun. One half of it is forever turned toward the Sun and is made bright by its rays, while the other half—shaded by its own bulk—remains dark, much like the side of a water pot <note>original: "kumbha"</note> placed in the sunlight. **(1)**

When the Sun's rays strike the watery surface of the Moon, the light is reflected, dispersing the darkness of the night, just as sunlight striking a mirror <note>original: "darpana"</note> illuminates the interior of a darkened house. **(2)**

As the Moon moves away from the Sun, its whiteness begins to appear from the western side. The extent of this visible light on the Moon's lower part increases daily, governed entirely by its distance from the Sun. **(3)**

In this manner, due to its specific position relative to the Sun, the Moon's brightness increases day by day. During the afternoon, this illumination grows on its western side, just as light gradually covers the surface of a jar. **(4)**

->**Predictions based on Lunar Path**<-

If the Moon <note>literally: "the cool-rayed one"</note> passes to the south of the constellations *Jyeshtha* <note>the Elder</note>, *Mula* <note>the Root</note>, or the two *Ashadhas*, it destroys seeds, aquatic animals, and forests, and brings the threat of fire. **(5)**

The Moon is considered inauspicious <note>original: "papa," meaning sinful or bringing evil</note> when it passes along the southern side of the constellations *Vishakha* and *Anuradha*.

When the moon takes the **form of a bow**, it foretells wars. In whichever direction the "bowstring" <note>The straight inner edge of the crescent</note> faces, those people will be victorious. When a continuous line forms a complete circle on all sides, it is known as the **"pot-shaped"** moon. In this event, local governors and kings will be forced to abandon their positions and territories. || 15 ||

In the absence of the previously mentioned positions, if the **northern horn is high**, it brings an increase in crops and plentiful rain. However, if the **southern horn is high**, the moon is said to indicate the fear of famine. || 16 ||

->The Great Compilation<-

If the Moon appears like ashes, rough, or reddish in body; if it is deprived of its rays, or if its form is dark, cracked, or flickering, it forebodes danger from hunger, war, disease, and thieves. <note>Verse 29: These "unnatural" appearances were viewed as atmospheric omens reflecting terrestrial instability.</note>

When the Moon appears as white as frost, the jasmine flower, the white water-lily, or crystal—as if it had been carefully polished by the Goddess Parvati <note>original: "Adrisutaya" (Daughter of the Mountain)</note> and held aloft in the night for my own welfare—then that Moon which is seen shall bring prosperity to the entire world. <note>Verse 30: A poetic invocation suggesting that a clear, bright moon is a divine blessing.</note>

If the Moon, as pale as a lotus stalk or a pearl necklace, wanes and waxes according to the fixed laws of the lunar days, and if its orb and rays follow their unceasing path, then the "Cold-Rayed One" <note>term: Sheeta-rashmi (a common epithet for the Moon in Sanskrit poetry)</note> brings victory to mankind. <note>Verse 31</note>

During the waxing fortnight, as the Moon increases, so too do the priests, the warriors, and the common subjects increase in prosperity. When the Moon wanes, they suffer loss; when it remains steady, they remain steady. In the dark fortnight, all these results are reversed. <note>Verse 32: This establishes the principle of "sympathetic magic" where the growth of the moon mirrors the growth of society.</note>

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 5: The Course of Rahu

Because it tasted the special sweetness of the nectar of immortality, it is said by some that this head of the Demon <note>The demon Swarbhanu, who was decapitated by Vishnu after drinking the nectar of the gods</note>, though severed from the body, did not lose its life force and became a planet. || 1 ||

Others claim that because it possesses the circular shape of the Moon and the Sun, and because it is dark in color, it cannot be seen in the sky except during the time of a conjunction <note>an eclipse</note>, owing to a boon granted by Brahma, the lotus-born creator. || 2 ||

Others teach that the body is divided into a face and a tail and has the form of a serpent. Yet another school of thought declares that the son of Simhika <note>Rahu</note> is formless and composed entirely of darkness. || 3 ||

If Rahu has a physical body and moves through the zodiac, or if he is simply a circular head, how could he—being fixed in his motion—seize the Sun or Moon when he is separated from them by exactly half a circle <note>180 degrees</note>? || 4 ||

If his motion were not fixed and predictable, how could his position be determined by mathematical calculation? Furthermore, if he is defined as having both a tail and a face, why does he not seize the luminaries in the interval between the two? || 5 ||

And if he has the form of a great serpent, he must seize with either his tail or his face...

<summary>In this passage, Varahamihira catalogs various mythological and physical theories regarding the nature of Rahu, the eclipse-causing shadow, before posing scientific challenges to the literal interpretation of the demon-myth.</summary>
<keywords>Rahu, eclipses, Indian astronomy, Varahamihira, planetary motion, mythology vs science, lunar nodes</keywords>

# The Great Compilation

->Page 25<-

> Because the Moon’s covering body <note>the Moon itself, acting as a shield</note> is large, it appears with blunt horns <note>the tips of the crescent</note> when it is half-covered. Because the covering body of the Sun <note>the Moon's shadow</note> is small, the Sun appears with sharp horns during an eclipse. || 12 ||

> In this way, the cause of eclipses has been explained by the ancient teachers who possessed divine sight. The traditional truth of the scriptures is that Rahu is the cause in this matter. || 13 ||

> Regarding that demon known as Rahu, a boon was granted to him by Brahma <note>the Creator deity</note>: "During an eclipse, your nourishment shall be provided by the portion of the offerings made into the sacred fire." || 14 ||

> At that time <note>during an eclipse</note>, his presence is near; therefore, the eclipse is metaphorically called 'Rahu.' Similarly, the northward and southward movement of the Moon is also treated as such in mathematical calculations. || 15 ||

> An eclipse can never be predicted by mere omens. Omens and portents of various forms occur at other times as well <note>without being followed by an eclipse</note>. || 16 ||

It is certainly not the case that an eclipse occurs simply due to the conjunction of five planets.

<summary>Varahamihira explains the visual geometry of solar and lunar eclipses while reconciling scientific observation with the mythological role of the demon Rahu. He emphasizes that eclipses must be determined by calculation rather than by relying on erratic omens or planetary groupings.</summary>

suffer the loss of their riches, yet there is an abundance of food. || 21 ||

An eclipse belonging to **Varuṇa** is inauspicious for the lords of the earth
but brings peace and the growth of crops for others.
An eclipse belonging to **Agni**, known as the "Friend,"
brings crops, health, fearlessness, and sufficient water. || 22 ||

If the eclipse occurs in the southern direction, it causes a lack of rain, famine, and the total destruction of crops. Any eclipse occurring beyond this point is considered inauspicious, bringing hunger, heavy burdens <note>original: "bhāra"; likely referring to excessive taxation or the weight of grief</note>, and drought. || 23 ||

If the eclipse occurs before the calculated time, it leads to miscarriages among women and the fury of the sword <note>warfare</note>. If it occurs after the calculated time, there will be a destruction of flowers and fruits, as well as general fear and the loss of crops. || 24 ||

The results of an eclipse occurring too early or too late have been stated here according to the observations of ancient scriptures. However, for a scholar who is an expert in accurate mathematics <term>Sphuta-ganita: the science of precise astronomical calculation</term>, the timing of the eclipse will never, under any circumstances, deviate from the calculation. || 25 ||

If both the Sun and the Moon are eclipsed within the same month, then the kings <note>original: "kṣitipāḥ"; literally 'protectors of the earth'</note> will meet their downfall due to the revolts of their own armies, and there will be intense outbreaks of war. || 26 ||

If the Sun or Moon rise or set while eclipsed, it brings destruction to the autumn crops and to the sovereign rulers. If they are completely eclipsed <note>a total eclipse</note> and are also under the influence of malefic planets, they bring famine and pestilence. || 27 ||

If they are eclipsed when only half-risen, it destroys the people of the Southwest <note>original: "Nairṛtikān"; those in the direction of the demon Nirṛti</note> and all forms of sacrificial rituals.

If the eclipse begins in the first part of the day, it destroys those who live by fire <note>original: "agnyupajīvi" - likely blacksmiths or priests performing sacrifices</note>, virtuous people, and Brahmins. <insert>It also affects those who follow the path of the Vedas.</insert> || 28 ||

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 5: The Transit of Rahu

If the darkness <note>Rahu, the shadow-demon</note> appears to lick the orb of the light-giver <note>the Sun or Moon</note> all around with a tongue, this is called **The Licking** (*Leha*). In this event, all living beings will be filled with joy, and the earth will be blessed with abundant waters. (45)

When a third, a quarter, or even a half of the orb is swallowed, it is called **The Seizing** (*Grasana*). This portends the loss of wealth for prosperous kings and brings suffering to flourishing nations. (46)

If the darkness seizes the outer edges but remains gathered in a thick mass in the center, it should be known as **The Obstruction** (*Nirodha*). This phenomenon brings delight to all living creatures. (47)

**The Crushing** (*Avamardana*) occurs when the darkness completely covers the orb and remains there for a long duration. This shadow-form destroys the most prominent nations and the most powerful kings. (48)

If, after the eclipse has ended, the darkness immediately returns to cover the orb again, it is called **The Mounting** (*Arohana*). This signifies danger to kings arising from mutual conflicts and wars. (49)

If a portion of the orb appears like a mirror obscured by the breath of a person... <note>The text breaks off here, describing the 'Virochana' or 'Shining' type of eclipse.</note>

<summary>Varāhamihira categorizes five specific types of eclipses—The Licking, Seizing, Obstruction, Crushing, and Mounting—detailing how their visual appearance predicts prosperity, war, or the downfall of rulers.</summary>

# [Chapter 5] The Great Compilation

If the eclipse appears the color of a pigeon, reddish-brown, tawny, or dark gray, one should predict the fear of famine. A pigeon-colored eclipse specifically affects the *Sudras* <note>The laboring or service class in traditional Indian society</note>, while a black-colored one brings about the spread of disease. ॥ 56 ॥

An eclipse with the yellow luster of a pure carnelian stone destroys the *Vaishyas* <note>The merchant and agricultural class</note> but simultaneously indicates a time of abundance and good food. If the eclipse appears to be emitting flames, there is a danger of fire; if it has the appearance of red chalk, expect wars to break out. ॥ 57 ॥

If it is dark green like a blade of *Durva* grass or yellow like turmeric, one should predict a plague. A Rahu <note>The celestial body responsible for eclipses in Vedic astronomy</note> that resembles the pale-red *Patala* flower brings the danger of lightning strikes. ॥ 58 ॥

When Rahu is seen with a dusty-red appearance, it leads to the destruction of the *Kshatriyas* <note>The warrior and ruling class</note>. If it bears the likeness of the rising sun, a lotus, or a rainbow, it provokes the fury of weapons <note>meaning an outbreak of armed conflict</note>. ॥ 59 ॥

If Mercury <note>original: "Saumya"</note> views the eclipsed body, it leads to a scarcity of ghee, honey, and oil, and brings trouble to kings. If Mars <note>original: "Bhauma"</note> views it, there will be the crushing weight of battle, the fury of fire, and fear of thieves. ॥ 60 ॥

If Venus <note>original: "Shukra"</note> views it, it causes the destruction of crops and brings various afflictions to the inhabitants of the earth.

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 5

<page-num>36</page-num>

An eclipse <note>referred to here as Rahu, the celestial demon responsible for seizing the sun and moon</note> occurring now brings distress to the people of Vanga, Anga, and Kashi <note>modern-day Bengal, Bihar, and Varanasi regions</note>. However, it also brings rain that meets the desires of the farming classes. **[72]**

An eclipse in the month of Phalguna <note>February–March</note> causes suffering to the people of Vanga, Ashmaka, Avanti, and Mekala. It likewise afflicts those skilled in dance, the finest of crops, noble women, archers, and those practicing austerities. **[73]**

In the month of Chaitra <note>March–April</note>, an eclipse brings distress to painters, scribes, singers, and those who live by their beauty <note>performers or models</note>. It also affects those knowledgeable in the Vedas, gold merchants, and the peoples of Pundra, Odra, Kaikaya, and Ashmaka. During this time, Indra <note>the lord of gods</note> provides a varied and unusual rainfall. **[74]**

Should an eclipse occur in the month of Vaishakha <note>April–May</note>, destruction comes to the crops of cotton, sesame, and mung beans. The tribes of the Ikshvakus, Yaudheyas, Shakas, and Kalingas will face calamities, though the period will otherwise be marked by an abundance of food. **[75]**

In the month of Jyeshtha <note>May–June</note>, kings, the priestly class, the wives of kings, crops, and great assemblies fall into ruin. Gentle men, the Salva people, and the tribes of the Nishadas <note>forest-dwelling hunters</note> are also destroyed, and the rains are affected. **[76]**

During an eclipse in the month of Ashadha <note>June–July</note>, wells, embankments, and the flow of rivers are disrupted, as are those who subsist on fruits and roots. The people of Gandhara, Kashmir, Pulinda, and China are said to be struck down, though there will be localized rainfall in various regions. **[77]**

# The Great Compilation <note>original: "Brihat Samhita"</note>
## Chapter 5

If an eclipse <note>referred to here as "the planet" or "the demon" Rahu</note> is seen during the month of **Shravana** <note>July–August</note>, it destroys the people of Kashmir, the Pulindas, the Chinese, the Greeks <note>original: "Yavana"</note>, the inhabitants of Kurukshetra, Gandhara, and the Middle Country. It also harms the Kambojas and whole-hoofed animals <note>such as horses</note>, as well as the autumn crops. Aside from these specific afflictions, the eclipse makes the rest of the earth covered with abundant food and joyful people. || 78 ||

The Demon <note>Rahu, the eclipse-causer</note> destroys the people of Kalinga, Vanga <note>Bengal</note>, Magadha, Surashtra, the barbarians <note>original: "Mlechha"</note>, the Sauvira, the Daradas, and the Shakas if he arrives in the month of **Bhadrapada** <note>August–September</note>. He also causes the loss of pregnancies in women, yet brings about a general state of plenty and prosperity despite these localized afflictions. || 79 ||

If the Demon is seen in the month of **Ashwayuja** <note>September–October</note>, he destroys the Kambojas, the Chinese, the Greeks, those who live by their weapons, and the inhabitants of the banks of the Bahlika and Indus rivers. He also harms the people of Anarta and Pundra, physicians, and the Kiratas <note>mountain tribes</note>. However, he also brings great abundance and prosperity to the land. || 80 ||

There are ten ways in which the Sun and Moon are released from an eclipse:
1. Breaking of the jaw <note>the eclipse clears from the side</note>
2. Breaking of the belly <note>clearing from the center</note>
3. Breaking of the anus <note>clearing from the bottom</note>
(Each of these occurs in two variations)
4. Vomiting <note>a rapid clearing</note>
5. Digestion <note>a slow clearing</note>
6. Splitting in the middle
7. Splitting at the end. || 81 ||

When the Moon exits toward the South-East, it is called the "Breaking of the Right Jaw." This results in the destruction of crops, diseases of the mouth, suffering for kings, but also brings good rainfall. || 82 ||

When the exit is toward the North-East, it is the "Breaking of the Left Jaw," which brings fear and danger to princes.

# The Great Compilation (Brihat Samhita) | [Chapter 5]

<page-num>38</page-num>

If the eclipse begins at the mouth, it foretells diseases of the face and danger from weapons <note>original: "shastra-bhayam"</note>; however, in that case, one may also expect an abundance of food <note>original: "subhiksham"</note>. || 83 ||

If the release of the eclipse <note>the moment the shadow leaves the moon or sun</note> occurs on the right side, it is known as a "Right-Belly-Piercing." This indicates suffering for princes and suggests that enemies to the south will be ready for an assault. || 84 ||

If the release occurs on the left side, and Rahu <note>the celestial shadow-demon responsible for eclipses</note> is positioned on the northern path, it is a "Left-Belly-Piercing." This brings the risk of miscarriage for women, and the harvests will be only mediocre. || 85 ||

If the shadow exits at the south-west or north-west corners, these are the two "Anus-Piercings," right and left respectively. These bring diseases of the private parts and poor harvests; specifically, if it occurs on the left, it foretells the death of a Queen. || 86 ||

When the eclipse begins on the eastern side and the shadow retreats toward the east as well, it is called "Vomiting" <note>original: "sac-chardanam"</note>. This is a benevolent omen, bringing safety, good crops, and joy to the world. || 87 ||

In an eclipse where the beginning is in the east but the retreat is toward the west, it is called "Decay" <note>original: "taj-jaranam"</note>. In such a time, people are distressed by hunger and the fear of weapons, wondering where they might find refuge. || 88 ||

<term>Rahu: In ancient Indian astronomy, the ascending node of the moon, personified as a shadow-demon that "swallows" the sun or moon during an eclipse.</term>
<term>Subhiksham: A state of plenty or a good harvest, the opposite of famine.</term>

# The Great Compilation [Chapter 5]

A harsh and powerful wind <note>original: "ruksho vayuh prabalashcha"</note> brings with it the fear of an outbreak of theft. **94**

If a solar eclipse occurs at the end of the same fortnight following a lunar eclipse, it leads to injustice among the people and mutual hostility between husbands and wives. **97**

However, if a lunar eclipse occurs after a solar eclipse, then the Brahmins <note>the priestly and scholarly class</note> will enjoy the fruits of many sacrifices, and the people will be truly joyful. **98**

If Mars begins its retrograde motion <note>vakra: the apparent backward movement of a planet</note> in the ninth, eighth, or seventh lunar mansion <note>nakshatra: the 27 divisions of the sky along the ecliptic</note> from its rising sign, that retrograde is called **"The Fiery"** (Ushna). Upon its rising, it brings suffering to those who work with fire <note>original: "agnivarttinam"; refers to blacksmiths, priests performing sacrifices, or cooks</note>. || 1 ||

When Mars <note>original: "Kuja"; a name for Mars meaning 'Son of the Earth'</note> turns retrograde in the twelfth, tenth, or eleventh lunar mansion, it is called **"The Tearful-Faced"** (Ashrumukha). Upon its rising, it spoils juices and liquids, and causes diseases and a lack of rain. || 2 ||

If it turns retrograde from the thirteenth or fourteenth lunar mansion, it is called **"The Cruel"** (Vyala) as it sets. It brings suffering from tusked animals, serpents, and wild beasts, yet it also brings a time of abundance <note>original: "subhiksham"; literally 'good alms' or plenty of food</note>. || 3 ||

When it turns back from the fifteenth or sixteenth lunar mansion, it is called **"The Blood-Faced"** (Rudhiranana). At that time, it brings diseases of the mouth and causes fear, yet it also brings about a good harvest. || 4 ||

If the retrograde occurs from the seventeenth or eighteenth lunar mansion, it is called **"The Sword and Club"** (Asimushala). It brings suffering from gangs of thieves, a lack of rain, and the fear of weapons. || 5 ||

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 7

The orbit known as **Natural** <note>original: "Prakrita"</note> consists of the constellations presided over by the Wind, Death, and the Great Ancestor <note>Vayu (Svati), Yama (Bharani), and Brahma (Rohini)</note>, as well as the Many <note>Krittika</note>. The **Mixed** <note>Mishra</note> motion is said to comprise the constellations of the Moon, Shiva, the Ancestors, the Serpent, and the Gods <note>Mrigashira, Ardra, Magha, Ashlesha, and Vishakha</note>. || 9 ||

In the **Shortened** <note>Sankshipta</note> orbit are the constellations of Nourishment <note>Pushya</note>, the Two Returners <note>Punarvasu</note>, and the two Fig Trees <note>Purva and Uttara Phalguni</note>. In the **Sharp** <note>Tikshna</note> orbit are the two Blessed Feet <note>Purva and Uttara Bhadrapada</note>, along with the constellations of Indra, the Horse-men, and the Nourisher <note>Jyeshtha, Ashwini, and Revati</note>. || 10 ||

The orbit called **End of Union** <note>Yogantika</note> includes the Root <note>Mula</note> and the two Invincible ones <note>Purva and Uttara Ashadha</note>; this is the motion of the Son of the Moon <note>term: "Suta-syendoh" - Mercury, who in Vedic mythology is the son of the Moon</note>. The **Terrible** <note>Ghora</note> orbit consists of Hearing, the Celestial Architect, the Wealthy Gods, and the Lord of Waters <note>Shravana, Chitra, Dhanishtha, and Shatabhisha</note>. || 11 ||

The orbit named **Evil** <note>Papa</note> includes the constellations of the Sun, the Friend, and the combined Indra-Agni <note>Hasta, Anuradha, and Vishakha</note>. He <note>referring to the sage Parashara</note> explained the characteristics of these motions based on the number of days the planet remains visible or invisible. || 12 ||

The durations for the orbits—beginning with the **Natural**—are forty, thirty, twenty-two, twenty, nine, nine, and fifteen days, followed by eleven days <note>These figures represent the periods Mercury remains visible after rising</note>. || 13 ||

During the **Natural** motion of Mercury, there is health, abundant rainfall, the flourishing of crops, and general well-being.

->Take the era of the Shaka King <note>The Shaka era, a historical calendar beginning in 78 CE</note>, add the appropriate additive,<-

# The Great Compilation
## [Chapter 8]

->The first four years are considered the best, the middle four are average, and the final four should be known as the lowest or least auspicious. [Verse 26]<-

When Jupiter <note>original: "Surejya," a title for Jupiter meaning 'Teacher of the Gods'</note> rises in the month of Magha <note>roughly January/February</note> having reached the first portion of the constellation Dhanishtha, the first year of the sixty-year cycle begins, known by the name **Prabhava**. This year functions for the welfare of all beings. [Verse 27]

In some places there may be a lack of rain, or distress caused by wind and fire; there may be calamities and diseases arising from phlegm <note>original: "shleshma," one of the three humors in Ayurvedic medicine</note>. Nevertheless, when this year **Prabhava** is active, the people do not suffer excessively. [Verse 28]

Following that, the second year is declared to be **Vibhava**, the third is **Shukla**, the fourth is **Pramoda**, and the fifth is **Prajapati**. In this sequence, each succeeding year is more auspicious, as are their respective harvests. [Verse 29]

During these years, the earth—the supporter of all beings—is ruled by the protector class <note>original: "Kshatra"</note>; it is filled with crops of ripened rice, sugarcane, and barley, freed from fears, with hostilities pacified, the people joyful, and liberated from the vices of the Dark Age <note>original: "Kali-dosha," referring to the spiritual decline associated with the Kali Yuga</note>. [Verse 30]

The second cycle of five years consists of **Angira**, **Shrimukha**, **Bhava**, **Yuva**, and **Dhata**. Among these five years in their proper order, the first three are considered excellent, while the remaining two are average. [Verse 31]

## [Chapter 8, Verses 32-36]

When Jupiter pierces the stars of the Great Bear <note>The Saptarishi constellation</note> and others, the gods grant rain according to desire, and the people remain free from disease and fear. In the following two years, there is likewise good and even rainfall; however, during this time, diseases and the onset of wars may occur. ॥ 32 ॥

In the cycle presided over by Indra <note>The Shakra Yuga</note>, the first year is called *Ishvara* and the second is *Bahudhanya* <note>meaning "Abundant Grain"</note>; these are said to be prosperous. Following these are the years *Pramathin* and *Vikrama*. One should understand the effects of these years through the specific movements of Jupiter. ॥ 33 ॥

The first and second years of this cycle are auspicious, creating a Golden Age <note>Krita Yuga</note> for the subjects. However, the year *Pramathin* is sinful, while *Vrisha* and *Vikrama* grant abundant food but also bring the fear of disease. ॥ 34 ॥

The first year of the fourth cycle, which they call *Chitrabhanu* <note>meaning "Bright Colored Sun"</note>, is considered the best. The second, named *Subhanu* <note>meaning "Beautiful Sun"</note>, is of middle quality; it brings some disease but is not fatal to the population. ॥ 35 ॥

After that comes *Tarana* <note>meaning "Crossing/Saving"</note>, which brings much rain, followed by *Parthiva*, which gladdens the world with the growth of crops. The fifth year is called *Vyaya* <note>meaning "Expenditure"</note>, which authorities desire as auspicious, characterized by the intensity of passion <note>Manmatha/Eros</note> and a multitude of festivals. ॥ 36 ॥

In the cycle presided over by Tvashtar <note>The celestial architect</note>, the first year is called *Sarvajit* <note>meaning "All-conquering"</note>, and the next is indeed *Sarvadhari* <note>meaning "All-supporting"</note>...

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 8

The first year in the ninth cycle <note>A cycle of five years is called a Yuga in this system</note> is called **Plavanga**; the next is **Kilaka**, followed by **Saumya**. Then comes **Sadharana**, and the final year is **Rodhakrit**. Among these, the years named **Kilaka** and **Saumya** bestow auspicious results. || 43 ||

The year **Plavanga** brings great suffering to many subjects. In **Sadharana**, there is scant rainfall and outbreaks of wandering plagues <note>The term 'iti' refers to the six traditional calamities of agriculture: drought, floods, locusts, rats, birds, and foreign invasion</note>. The fifth year, known as **Rodhakrit**, brings varied rainfall and a rich abundance of crops. || 44 ||

The tenth cycle is presided over by the dual deities Indra and Agni <note>The gods of thunder and fire</note>. Its first year is named **Paridhavin**, followed by **Pramadi**, then **Ananda**, then **Rakshasa**, and finally the year named **Anala**. || 45 ||

During **Paridhavin**, there is destruction in the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha, the central heartland of ancient India</note>, the loss of kings, meager rainfall, and danger from fire. In the year named **Pramadi**, people become lazy, and there is civil unrest as well as the destruction of red-colored flowers and seeds. || 46 ||

The year following that, **Ananda**, brings joy to all the world. **Rakshasa** and **Anala**, however, are destructive. Specifically, **Rakshasa** promotes the growth of summer crops but **Anala** <note>Anala is a name for Fire</note> brings danger from fire and the spread of fatal epidemics. || 47 ||

In the eleventh cycle, the years are **Pingala**, **Kalayukta**, **Siddhartha**, **Raudra**, and indeed **Durmati**.

### Verse 17

The fifth circle, beginning with the star Jyeshtha and comprising five lunar mansions <note>Jyeshtha, Mula, Purva Ashadha, Uttara Ashadha, and Shravana</note>, brings distress through hunger, thieves, and disease. It specifically afflicts the people of Kashmir, Ashmaka, Matsya, the Charudevis, and Avanti.

### Verse 18

When Venus ascends in this circle, it destroys the Abhiras, the Dravidians, the Ambasthas, the Trigartas, and the Saurashtrians <note>People of the Gujarat peninsula</note>. It also brings ruin to the people of Sindh and Sauvira, and the death of the King of Kashi <note>Modern-day Varanasi</note>.

### Verse 19

The sixth circle, consisting of six lunar mansions beginning with Dhanishtha <note>Dhanishtha, Shatabhisha, Purva Bhadrapada, Uttara Bhadrapada, Revati, and Ashwini</note>, is generally auspicious. It results in an abundance of wealth and thriving herds of cattle, with plentiful grain, though there may be fear in some isolated places.

### Verse 20

However, if Venus should ascend abnormally in this circle, the Shulikas, the Gandharas <note>Region of modern-day Afghanistan/Pakistan</note>, and the people of Avanti are oppressed. There is the death of the King of Videha, while the border tribes, the Yavanas <note>Greeks or western foreigners</note>, the Shakas <note>Scythians</note>, and the servant classes see an increase in their power.

### Verse 21

In the western sky, the circles beginning with Swati and Jyeshtha are considered auspicious. In the eastern sky, the circle beginning with Magha <note>referred to here as Pitrya, the star of the Ancestors</note> is auspicious. The remaining circles yield the specific fruits previously described.

### Verse 22

If Venus is seen while the sun has not yet set, it brings fear and causes minor diseases for the entire day. If it is seen during the midday along with the moon, it causes the destruction of the king's army and the city. || 23 ||

When the "Cart of Rohini" <note>original: "prajapatye shakate" - a specific V-shaped formation in the constellation Taurus</note> is pierced by Venus, the earth—as if having committed a great sin—bears a resemblance to the Kapalika penance <note>A radical ascetic practice involving the carrying of a skull</note>, becoming covered with pieces of hair and bone. || 25 ||

Friends no longer abide in the spirit of friendship, and the **Twice-born** <note>the priestly or scholarly classes</note> no longer remain devoted to their proper rituals.

> While passing through the mansions presided over by the Serpent, Varuna, or Indra <note>Ashlesha, Shatabhisha, and Vishakha</note>, he brings great safety but not much rain. > When the Son of the Sun is in Krittika, those who live by fire <note>such as blacksmiths or priests</note> and army commanders are tormented.

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 10

When the star **Rohini** <note>The fourth lunar mansion, associated with the star Aldebaran</note> is afflicted, the following are affected: the people of **Kosala**, **Madra**, **Kashi**, and **Panchala**, as well as those who travel by carts. **[4]**

Under **Mrigashira** <note>The fifth lunar mansion, 'The Deer's Head'</note>: the inhabitants of **Vatsa**, those who perform sacrifices, the patrons of such sacrifices, the noble people <note>original: "Aryajana"</note>, and the populations of the **Middle Country** <note>The central region of Northern India</note>.
When the star of **Rudra** <note>Ardra, the sixth lunar mansion</note> is occupied: the **Paratas**, the **Ramathas**, oil-millers, washermen, and thieves. **[5]**

Under **Aditi** <note>Punarvasu, the seventh lunar mansion</note>: the people of the **Five Rivers** <note>The Punjab region</note>, the borderlands, **Surashtra**, **Sindhu**, and **Sauvira**.
Under **Pushya** <note>The eighth lunar mansion</note>: bell-ringers, heralds, **Yavanas** <note>Greeks or Westerners</note>, merchants, gamblers, and flowers. **[6]**

Under the **Serpent star** <note>Ashlesha, the ninth lunar mansion</note>: aquatic products and snakes.
Under the **Ancestral star** <note>Magha, the tenth lunar mansion</note>: the people of **Balkh**, **China**, and **Gandhara**; also the **Shulikas**, the **Paratas**, the merchant caste, granaries, and traders. **[7]**

Under **Bhagya** <note>Purva Phalguni, the eleventh lunar mansion</note>: those who sell liquids, prostitutes, young maidens, and the **Maharashtrians**.
Under **Aryaman** <note>Uttara Phalguni, the twelfth lunar mansion</note>: kings, molasses, salt, beggars, water, and the city of **Taxila**. **[8]**

Under **Hasta** <note>The thirteenth lunar mansion</note>: barbers, oil-pressers <note>or those who travel by wheels</note>, thieves, physicians, tailors, elephant-catchers, harlots, the people of **Kosala**, and garland-makers are afflicted. **[9]**

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 11

> A planet that shines with the pure luster of a cat's-eye gem <note>original: "vaidūrya"; a chrysoberyl or beryl</note> brings blessings to the people. One that resembles the color of a sharp arrow or the blue flax flower <note>original: "atasī"; Linum usitatissimum</note> is also considered auspicious. > Having examined the teachings of Garga on the "Movement of the Crested Ones" <note>original: "shikhichāra"; referring to comets or "crested" stars</note>, as well as the works of Parashara, Asita, and Devala, and many others besides, this clear and uncomplicated account of their movements is now composed. || 1 ||

> Their appearance or disappearance cannot be calculated through mathematical methods alone. This is because Comets <note>original: "ketus"; refers to a wide range of celestial portents including comets, meteors, and atmospheric phenomena</note> are of three distinct types: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial. || 2 ||

> When a form resembling fire appears where there is no actual fuel or flame, it is declared to be a "Ketu"—excluding, however, the light of fireflies, the phosphorescence of ghosts <note>original: "pishāca-ālaya"; likely referring to ignis fatuus or "will-o'-the-wisp"</note>, and the natural radiance of gems and jewels. || 3 ||

> Those that appear upon banners, weapons, houses, trees, horses, or elephants are known as atmospheric portents.

# The Great Compilation
## [Chapter 11]

Comets that appear among the stars are considered divine; those that appear otherwise <note>original: "bhāumāḥ"; referring to atmospheric or terrestrial phenomena</note> are considered earthly. These are the different types of "crested" stars <note>original: "shikhinaḥ"; a term for comets referring to their tails or crests</note>. || 4 ||

Some authorities state there are one hundred and one comets; others claim there are one thousand. However, the sage Narada <note>A legendary divine sage in Indian tradition known for his knowledge of the cosmos</note> has declared that there is only one Comet, which manifests in many different forms. || 5 ||

Whether there is only one or many, the results must be predicted in all cases based on their rising and setting, their positions in the sky, their contacts with stars, their smoke-like tails, and their colors. || 6 ||

The duration of the comet's effects corresponds to the number of days it remains visible: for every day it is seen, the results will ripen for one month. If it is visible for months, the results will last for years. These effects begin to manifest after the first fortnight <note>A period of fifteen days</note> has passed. || 7 ||

A comet that is short, thin, clear, glossy, straight, white, and remains visible for only a short time brings abundance and happiness when it rises or is sighted. || 8 ||

A "smoke-bannered" comet <note>original: "dhūmaketu"</note> that possesses characteristics opposite to those mentioned above is not auspicious. This is especially true if it resembles a rainbow or possesses two crests <note>tails</note>. || 9 ||

<term>Brihat Samhita: The "Great Compilation" of Varahamihira, a foundational 6th-century text on astrology and natural omens.</term>
<term>Ketu: A celestial body or comet; in Indian astronomy, it often refers to the descending node of the moon or a tailed star.</term>
<term>Narada: An ancient sage credited with early astronomical observations.</term>
<term>Nakshatra: The lunar mansions or star clusters used as a map of the sky.</term>
<term>Phalapaka: The "ripening of fruits," referring to the timing and manifestation of predicted karmic results.</term>
<term>Dhumaketu: Literally "smoke-bannered," a common Sanskrit term for a comet.</term>
<term>Shikhin: "The crested one," a synonym for a comet or fire.</term>

# The Great Compilation
## [Chapter 11]

Those known as the "Ray-bearers" are twenty-five in number, appearing like strings of pearls, jewels, or gold, and possessing crests. They are visible in the East and the West; these **sons of the Sun** <note>original: "ravijāḥ"</note> bring about conflicts between kings. || 10 ||

Resembling parrots, fire, the Bandhujiva flower <note>a bright red flower, Pentapetes phoenicea</note>, lac-dye, or blood are the **sons of Fire**. There are also twenty-five of these, appearing in the South-East; they bring the danger of outbreaks of fire. || 11 ||

The **sons of Death** have curved crests and appear rough and black in color; they are also twenty-five in number. They are seen in the Southern direction and announce the coming of pestilence among the people. || 12 ||

Circular like a mirror, without tails but endowed with rays, are the twenty-two **sons of the Earth**. They appear in the North-East and resemble water or oil in luster; they bring the fear of famine. || 13 ||

Resembling moonbeams, silver, snow, the white water-lily, or the Kunda flower <note>a type of white jasmine</note> are the **sons of the Moon**. These three crested comets appear in the North and bring about times of abundance and prosperity. || 14 ||

The **son of Brahma** is but one, possessing three crests and three colors; he appears only to bring about the end of an age <note>original: "yugāntakara," referring to the cataclysmic end of a cosmic cycle</note>.

# Brihat Samhita | [Chapter 11]

->Page 72<-

Those comets which appear in no fixed direction and possess a variety of colors are known as the **Staffs of Brahma** <note>original: "Brahmadanda"; these are considered highly significant and unpredictable omens</note>. || 15 ||

One hundred and one comets have been described thus far; now, I shall explain the distinct characteristics of the remaining nine hundred comets. || 16 ||

The eighty-four comets known as the **Sons of Venus** <note>original: "Shukrasuta"</note> appear in the north or north-east. They possess large, white stars and are glossy in appearance; they bring about intense and powerful consequences. || 17 ||

The sixty comets born from **Saturn** <note>original: "Shanaishcharangaruha"</note> are glossy, radiant, and possess two tails. They are known by the name **Golden** <note>original: "Kanaka"</note>; they are visible throughout the sky and their effects are extremely painful and difficult to endure. || 18 ||

The sixty-five comets known as the **Hairless** <note>original: "Vikacha"</note> are the **Sons of Jupiter** <note>original: "Gurusuta"</note>. They consist of a single white star and lack a visible tail. They appear in the south, are glossy in texture, and are considered malevolent in their influence. || 19 ||

The fifty-one comets born of **Mercury** <note>original: "Budhaja"</note> are known as the **Thieves** <note>original: "Taskara"</note>. They are not very distinct, appearing thin, long, and white. They can appear in any direction and their effects are consistently evil. || 20 ||

# [Chapter 11]
->The Great Compilation<-

There are sixty sons of Mars <note>original: "Kujatmajāḥ"; referring to comets associated with the planet Mars</note> who resemble blood and fire in appearance. They appear as three-pronged stars <note>resembling a trident or trisula</note> and are known by the name Saffron-colored. Located in the northern quarter, they are portents of evil. || 21 ||

There are thirty-three others belonging to Rahu <note>the shadow planet responsible for eclipses</note>, famously known as the Dark Bolts <note>original: "Tāmasa-kīlakāḥ"</note>. They are seen appearing upon the discs of the Sun and the Moon; the results of their appearance are the same as those described for the transit of the Sun. || 22 ||

There are another one hundred and twenty comets named "Universal Forms" <note>original: "Viśvarūpa"</note> belonging to Agni <note>the god of Fire</note>. Their bodies are entangled in garlands of flames, and they bestow the fear of terrible conflagrations. || 23 ||

There are seventy-seven comets belonging to Vayu <note>the god of the Wind</note> known as the "Ruddy Ones." They are dark red, starless, shaped like a chowrie <note>a fly-whisk used in royal ceremonies</note>, and possess scattered rays. They are harsh and bringers of misfortune. || 24 ||

There are eight comets belonging to Prajapati <note>the Creator Lord</note> named the "Calculators" <note>original: "Gaṇakāḥ"</note>, which resemble a cluster of stars. There are also two hundred and four comets known as the "Offspring of Brahma," which are square in shape. || 25 ||

There are thirty-two comets born of Varuna <note>the god of the Waters</note> named "Herons" <note>original: "Kaṅkāḥ"</note>; they appear in the form of clumps of brushwood.

# The Great Compilation
## Chapter 11

->Page 75<-

In the eastern direction, appearing in the path of Agni <note>The "Path of Fire" refers to a specific longitudinal division of the sky in Vedic astronomy</note>, is the comet named **Raudra** <note>The Terrible One</note>. It resembles the tip of a trident, and its light is dusky, rough, and copper-colored. It spans one-third of the sky, and its effects are as calamitous as those of the *Kapala* comet <note>The "Skull" comet, previously described as causing famine and death</note>. || 32 ||

In the western direction appears the comet **Chalaketu** <note>The Trembling Comet</note>. Its crest is a mere finger’s breadth in height and points toward the south. As it moves further toward the north, it increases in length. || 33 ||

After touching the Seven Sages <note>The constellation Ursa Major or the Big Dipper</note>, the Pole Star <note>Sanskrit: Dhruva</note>, and the star Abhijit <note>Vega</note>, it turns back. Having traversed half the sky, it eventually sets in the southern direction. || 34 ||

This comet brings destruction to the regions stretching from the banks of the Prayaga <note>Modern-day Prayagraj/Allahabad</note> to Avanti <note>The region around Ujjain</note>, the Pushkara forests, and the lands near the Devika River. It especially afflicts the region known as the Middle Country <note>Sanskrit: Madhyadesha; the heartland of Indo-Aryan culture</note>. || 35 ||

It also strikes other various countries here and there with disease and famine. The ripening of its karmic fruits <note>The duration of its effects</note> lasts for ten months, though some authorities claim it lasts for eighteen. || 36 ||

Visible in the first half of the night, with its crest pointing south, is another comet known as **Shvetaketu** <note>The White Comet</note>.

# The Great Compilation
### [Chapter 11]

Others describe the comet named **Ka** as having the shape of a yoke <note>original: "yugākṛti"; a wooden bar used to harness oxen</note>; these two appear simultaneously and remain visible for seven days. || 37 ||

If they appear glossy, they bring abundance and well-being. However, if the one named **Ka** remains visible for a longer duration, it creates distress for ten years caused by the outbreak of weapons <note>original: "śastraprakopa"; signifying war or armed conflict</note>. || 38 ||

The comet known as **The White One** <note>original: "Śveta"</note> appears with the form of matted hair <note>original: "jaṭākāra"</note>. It is rough, dark-brown, and occupies one-third of the sky. It retreats in an anti-clockwise direction <note>original: "apasavya"</note> and destroys all but a third of the population. || 39 ||

When a comet appears in the constellation of the **Pleiades** <note>original: "Kṛttikā"</note> with a smoky tail, it should be known as the **Radiant Comet** <note>original: "Raśmiketu"</note>. It bears the same results as the White Comet mentioned above. || 40 ||

The **Constant Comet** <note>original: "Dhruvaketu"</note> is one whose path, size, color, and shape are not fixed; it appears everywhere. It may belong to the celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial regions. When it is glossy, it yields desirable results. || 41 ||

This comet appears upon the components of a King's army, upon the houses, trees, and mountains of various countries, and upon the household utensils of those destined for destruction. || 42 ||

# [Chapter 11] The Great Compilation

The comet known as **Kumuda** <note>literally "White Water-lily"</note> possesses the luster of a white lily. It appears in the western sky with its tail pointing toward the east for a single night. When sighted, it brings about incomparable abundance and prosperity <term>Subhiksha: a period of plenty and easy access to food</term> for a period of ten years. ॥ 43 ॥

The comet named **Maniketu** <note>literally "Jewel-Banner"</note> is visible for only a single watch <term>Yama: a three-hour period</term> in the west. It has a very small, fine star for its head. Its tail is straight, white, and rises from the head like a stream of milk sprayed from a breast. ॥ 44 ॥

As soon as it rises, this comet creates a period of abundance lasting four and a half months. However, it also frequently causes the mass appearance of small, troublesome creatures <note>likely referring to pests or stinging insects</note>. ॥ 45 ॥

There is also **Jalaketu** <note>literally "Water-Banner"</note>, which appears in the west with a glossy, upward-pointing tail. It brings nine months of abundance and ensures peace and tranquility for the people of the world. ॥ 46 ॥

**Bhavaketu** <note>literally "Existence-Banner"</note> is visible for only one night in the east. It has a tiny star and a glossy appearance. Its tail resembles the tail of a lion and curves in a clockwise direction. ॥ 47 ॥

For as many moments <term>Muhurta: a unit of time roughly equal to 48 minutes</term> as this comet remains visible in the sky, one should predict an equal number of months of its influence.

# Brihat Samhita | [Chapter 11]

> ...so long shall there be incomparable abundance <note>original: "subhikṣaṃ"; a period of plenty and easy access to food</note>.
